query:
How sensitive are EBSD-derived microstructural measurements to acquisition and post-processing parameter choices, and what does the literature report about the resulting uncertainty, bias, and reproducibility?

Cover specifically:
1. Quantified sensitivity studies: how much do reported grain size, grain count, texture strength/ODF intensity, KAM, GND density, low-angle vs high-angle grain boundary fractions, and grain boundary character distribution change as a function of step size, angular/orientation precision, indexing method (Hough vs dictionary indexing vs refinement), misorientation tolerance for grain reconstruction, minimum grain size cutoff, confidence-index or fit thresholding, and noise-reduction/cleanup operations (grain dilation, neighbour orientation correlation, neighbour pattern averaging)?
2. Documented bias: which cleanup and filtering operations are known to systematically bias grain size, texture, KAM/GND, or boundary statistics, and by how much? What reporting is required or recommended by standards and by the community (ASTM E2627, ISO 13067, round-robin or interlaboratory studies)?
3. Uncertainty quantification: what work exists on assigning uncertainty or confidence intervals to EBSD-derived grain size, texture, and misorientation-based metrics, including the number of grains required for statistically meaningful grain size and texture measurements?
4. Interlaboratory reproducibility: are there round-robin studies, benchmark datasets, or reproducibility assessments comparing EBSD results across labs, vendors, or software packages? What discrepancies were found?
5. Community consensus: what practices are recommended as best practice for reporting EBSD post-processing so results are reproducible, and where does the literature explicitly call for more automated, objective, or reproducible parameter selection?

Give explicit citations and quantitative numbers wherever the literature reports them.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions

        - DEVICE: Device interventions

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: How sensitive are EBSD-derived microstructural measurements to acquisition and post-processing parameter choices, and what does the literature report about the resulting uncertainty, bias, and reproducibility?

Cover specifically:
1. Quantified sensitivity studies: how much do reported grain size, grain count, texture strength/ODF intensity, KAM, GND density, low-angle vs high-angle grain boundary fractions, and grain boundary character distribution change as a function of step size, angular/orientation precision, indexing method (Hough vs dictionary indexing vs refinement), misorientation tolerance for grain reconstruction, minimum grain size cutoff, confidence-index or fit thresholding, and noise-reduction/cleanup operations (grain dilation, neighbour orientation correlation, neighbour pattern averaging)?
2. Documented bias: which cleanup and filtering operations are known to systematically bias grain size, texture, KAM/GND, or boundary statistics, and by how much? What reporting is required or recommended by standards and by the community (ASTM E2627, ISO 13067, round-robin or interlaboratory studies)?
3. Uncertainty quantification: what work exists on assigning uncertainty or confidence intervals to EBSD-derived grain size, texture, and misorientation-based metrics, including the number of grains required for statistically meaningful grain size and texture measurements?
4. Interlaboratory reproducibility: are there round-robin studies, benchmark datasets, or reproducibility assessments comparing EBSD results across labs, vendors, or software packages? What discrepancies were found?
5. Community consensus: what practices are recommended as best practice for reporting EBSD post-processing so results are reproducible, and where does the literature explicitly call for more automated, objective, or reproducible parameter selection?

Give explicit citations and quantitative numbers wherever the literature reports them.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

function.arguments: {"plan_json": "{\"objectives\":[{\"id\":1,\"objective\":\"Identify standards, reviews, and quantified EBSD sensitivity studies covering acquisition and post-processing Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Systematic discrepancies persist between results from grain size measurement standards, such as ASTM E 112 and ASTM E 2627, when different imaging techniques and analysis methods are used. The source of these discrepancies may be differences in imaging physics, resolution limits, grain boundary definitions, post-processing practices, or combinations thereof. Geometric distortions and drift effects in scanning electron microscope imaging are systematically modeled using synthetic microstructures to assess their impact on electron backscatter diffraction-based grain size measurement accuracy. Standard methods are compared to a lesser-known method, the Triple Point Count (TPC). Most distortion types introduce smaller biases than the expected accuracy of the methods under typical imaging conditions. TPC provides consistent performance across varying resolutions and sampling conditions. This provides further evidence that reported discrepancies are largely driven by an assumption made in the estimate for converting intercept measurements to ASTM grain size numbers, as recently reported by Evans et al.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Generating reduced-order, synthetic grain structure datasets that accurately represent the measured grain structure of a material is important for reducing the cost and increasing the accuracy of computational crystal plasticity efforts. This study introduces a machine-learning-based approach, termed texture adaptive clustering and sampling (TACS), for generating representative Euler angle datasets that accurately mimic the crystallographic texture. The TACS approach employs K-means clustering and density-based sampling in a closed-loop iteration to create representative Euler angle datasets. Proof-of-principle experiments were performed on rolled and recrystallized low-carbon steel. Validation of the TACS approach was extended to twenty-two datasets, varying lattice structures, and complex crystallographic textures, thereby encompassing a broad range of materials and crystal structures. Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test comparisons underscore the performance of the TACS approach over traditional electron backscatter diffraction EBSD dataset reduction techniques, with average K-S test scores nearing 0.9, indicating a high-fidelity representation of the original datasets. In contrast, conventional methods display scores below 0.3, indicating less reliability of the structure representation. The independence of the TACS approach from material texture and its capability to autonomously generate datasets with predetermined data points demonstrates its unbiased potential in streamlining dataset preparation for crystallographic analysis.

The excerpt addresses sensitivity and uncertainty of EBSD-derived grain size measurements across different software packages (AZtecCrystal, OIM Analysis, MTEX 6.0.0) using identical grain boundary threshold angles of 10°. Key findings include: number-weighted metrics show ±26-100% variation with different clean-up methods, while area-weighted metrics are more robust at ±0.2-10% variation. Clean-up routines must comply with ISO 13067 (≤5% change) or ASTM E2627 (≤10% change). Grain area computation method uncertainty is comparable to clean-up effects but has negligible impact on mean free distance (MFD). Standards specify minimum grain size thresholds of 10 points (ISO 13067) or 100 points (ASTM E2627) for exclusion. Edge grain exclusion causes underestimation of area-weighted grain size in small maps, particularly when grain sizes are large relative to map field of view. The Miles-Lantejoul correction is recommended by ISO 13067 to account for edge bias but is complex to implement in additively manufactured microstructures with variable grain shapes.

The excerpt provides evidence on EBSD grain size measurement uncertainty and reproducibility. Grain clean-up uncertainty varies significantly with indexing rate: ±13% for 65% indexed maps versus ±4% for 95% indexed maps. EBSD step size and grain boundary threshold angle are critical interdependent parameters that must be identical for valid grain size comparisons. ISO 13067 recommends step sizes around 10% of average grain diameter, while 20% recommendations from other sources are insufficient for additive manufacturing structures. Unindexed points disproportionately affect small grain measurement due to non-random spatial distribution. Sample selection bias appears significant, with participants in interlaboratory studies disagreeing on whether to exclude fine grains near AM build surfaces. These factors collectively impact reproducibility of average grain size measurements from EBSD data.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32'.

KP Mingard, PN Quested, and MS Peck. Determination of grain size by ebsd-report on a round robin measurement of equiaxed titanium. Unknown journal, 2012.

This interlaboratory round-robin study on titanium grain size measurement via EBSD identified critical sensitivity to multiple parameters. Four of twelve laboratories reported significantly different results. Key error sources included: magnification calibration errors, noise reduction/data cleanup procedures, and step size selection with insufficient mapped area causing larger grains to be missed. After outlier removal, reproducibility standard deviation was 1.98 µm for equivalent circle diameter and 1.15 µm for linear intercept, with 10% lower values for linear intercept measurements. Smallest grain size cutoff choice was identified as the main source of interlaboratory variation, with disproportionate effects from small grains. Calibration and tilt angle measurement errors perpendicular to the tilt axis contributed to area-based measurements. Acceptable indexing was achieved at approximately 80% rather than the stated 95% target. The study emphasized proper reporting of grain size distribution data and cutoff values in both pixels and micrometers.

This excerpt provides quantitative guidance on EBSD grain size measurement uncertainty and reproducibility for additively manufactured materials. Key parameter sensitivities include: EBSD step size should be ~10% of average grain diameter (per ISO 13067), though 20% is too coarse for AM structures with non-convex grains. Field of view (FoV) significantly affects sampling uncertainty—20 grain lengths per FoV achieves ~10% sampling uncertainty, which dominates total combined uncertainty. Random sampling uncertainty is the primary uncertainty component. The indexed-area-weighted median minimum Feret diameter (MFD) is recommended as the primary grain size statistic. EBSD map clean-up operations can change orientations by up to 5%. A relative combined expanded uncertainty (k=2) of 20% is achievable. Grain boundary threshold angle and EBSD step size must be reported when sub-grain structure or intragranular misorientations are present. Edge grains should be excluded. Small grain exclusion requires documenting their indexed area fraction. FoV should be at least 20× larger than median grain length to avoid discrete jumps in cumulative histograms at the 50% median point.

The excerpt presents quantitative evidence on EBSD grain size measurement sensitivity and uncertainty. Key findings include: sampling requirements of 300-500 grains reduce variability and flatten curves, with ASTM E 112 recommending minimum 50 grains for planimetric methods or 50 intercepts. Under typical SEM/optical microscopy conditions, distortions cause negligible bias, with most methods showing ΔG variations within ±0.5 G, within acceptable standard tolerances. However, sensitivity varies by method: Abrams and Heyn intercept-based methods show largest sensitivity with increases up to ±2 G under drift conditions, while planimetric methods show ~1 G changes and TPC/ASTM E 2627 show smallest changes. Two-directional drift (x and y) produces greater variation than single-direction drift. The TPC method demonstrates superior robustness to distortion and scan resolution changes compared to intercept-based approaches, making it a potentially reliable alternative for conditions with large drift or imaging distortions.

From text 'muirhead2001themorphologicalcharacterisation pages 37-43'.

JJ Muirhead. The morphological characterisation of grains and grain boundaries. Unknown journal, 2001.

The excerpt provides quantitative evidence on EBSD sensitivity and reproducibility across multiple parameters. Angular resolution depends on pixel resolution and calibration—calibration errors of 2-3° can cause incorrect boundary categorization. Misorientation angle accuracy shows dependency on angle magnitude: measurements of 20° or greater are within 5° of true value, while smaller misorientations have larger error magnitudes. Spatial resolution varies with material and orientation: 50-150nm parallel to tilt axis versus 150-500nm perpendicular for aluminum; lighter materials exhibit worse spatial resolution due to electron beam penetration. System angular accuracy of ±0.5° was insufficient to detect texture changes at medium amplitudes. Beam current optimization affects indexing accuracy and spatial resolution—low currents produce poorly-defined Kikuchi lines causing indexing failures, while high currents limit resolution through beam size and penetration depth. Cold work tolerance is minimal for subsequent EBSD analysis. Grain size perception is affected by boundary visibility—fewer visible boundaries cause grains to appear larger. Calibration reproducibility and specimen preparation are critical for quantitative investigations.

This round-robin study of 12 laboratories measuring equiaxed titanium grain size via EBSD provides quantitative reproducibility and uncertainty data. Equivalent circle diameter measurements showed approximately 10% higher values than linear intercept measurements. Reproducibility limits for equivalent circle diameter were 80% greater than for linear intercept methods, attributed to calibration drift and tilt correction errors. Four of 12 laboratories reported results significantly differing from the mean. Repeatability (within single laboratory) was substantially better than reproducibility (between laboratories). The choice of minimum grain size cutoff proved most critical to reported values, with smallest grains disproportionately affecting averages depending on step size, data quality, and treatment of poorly indexed points. Processing parameters identified as significant include magnification, minimum grain size specification, and map noise cleanup.

The excerpt addresses sensitivity and reproducibility of EBSD grain size measurements in additively manufactured materials. Key findings include: EBSD average grain size measurements are extremely sensitive to operator choices in experimental design, data clean-up, grain reconstruction, and statistical analysis. Critical parameters and their effects are documented: (1) Small grain removal (< 10-100 points per grain) severely biases results; (2) Step size should be 20 points per grain (20% of average diameter), not 80-500 points; (3) Map quality must exceed 90% indexed fraction, as unindexed points along boundaries artificially fragment or link grains; (4) Misorientation threshold of 10° is more appropriate than 5° for sub-grain structures; (5) Field of view should match grain aspect ratio; (6) Statistics should use log-normal or Weibull distributions rather than Gaussian; (7) Area-weighted means are preferable to number-weighted means which underestimate grain size. Abstract:
High angular resolution electron backscatter diffraction (HR-EBSD) affords an increase in angular resolution, as compared to ‘conventional’ Hough transform based EBSD, of two orders of magnitude, enabling measurements of relative misorientations of 1 x 10−4 rads (~ 0.006°) and changes in (deviatoric) lattice strain with a precision of 1 x 10−4. This is achieved through direct comparison of two or more diffraction patterns using sophisticated cross-correlation based image analysis routines. Image shifts between zone axes in the two-correlated diffraction pattern are measured with sub-pixel precision and this realises the ability to measure changes in interplanar angles and lattice orientation with a high degree of sensitivity. These shifts are linked to strains and lattice rotations through simple geometry. In this manuscript, we outline the basis of the technique and two case studies that highlight its potential to tackle real materials science challenges, such as deformation patterning in polycrystalline alloys.

## 2. High‐Angular Resolution Electron Backscatter Diffraction as a New Tool for Mapping Lattice Distortion in Geological Minerals

Abstract:
Analysis of distortions of the crystal lattice within individual mineral grains is central to the investigation of microscale processes that control and record tectonic events. These distortions are generally combinations of lattice rotations and elastic strains, but a lack of suitable observational techniques has prevented these components being mapped simultaneously and routinely in earth science laboratories. However, the technique of high‐angular resolution electron backscatter diffraction (HR‐EBSD) provides the opportunity to simultaneously map lattice rotation and elastic strain gradients with exceptional precision, on the order of 0.01° for rotations and 10−4 in strain, using a scanning electron microscope. Importantly, these rotations and lattice strains relate to densities of geometrically necessary dislocations and residual stresses. Recent works have begun to apply and adapt HR‐EBSD to geological minerals, highlighting the potential of the technique to provide new insights into the microphysics of rock deformation. Therefore, the purpose of this review is to provide a summary of the technique, to identify caveats and targets for further development, and to suggest areas where it offers potential for major advances. In particular, HR‐EBSD is well suited to characterizing the roles of different dislocation types during crystal plastic deformation and to mapping heterogeneous internal stress fields associated with specific deformation mechanisms/microstructures or changes in temperature, confining pressure, or macroscopic deviatoric stress. These capabilities make HR‐EBSD a particularly powerful new technique for analyzing the microstructures of deformed geological materials.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) has traditionally relied upon methods such as the Hough transform and dictionary Indexing to interpret diffraction patterns and extract crystallographic orientation. However, these methods encounter significant limitations, particularly when operating at high scanning speeds, where the exposure time per pattern is decreased beyond the operating sensitivity of CCD camera. Hence the signal to noise ratio decreases for the observed pattern which makes the pattern noisy, leading to reduced indexing accuracy. This research work aims to develop generative machine learning models for the post-processing or on-the-fly processing of Kikuchi patterns which are capable of restoring noisy EBSD patterns obtained at high scan speeds. These restored patterns can be used for the determination of crystal orientations to provide reliable indexing results. We compare the performance of such generative models in enhancing the quality of patterns captured at short exposure times (high scan speeds). An interesting observation is that the methodology is not data-hungry as typical machine learning methods.</jats:p>

## 1. currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 1-3 (Context ID: pqac-00000008)

Towards an Integrated Texture Toolkit, 1: Unveiling the Complex Relationship Between Crystal Size,
                               Shape, and Fabric in EBSD Data

                     Ryan M., Currier*1, Tushar Mittal2, Paulo J., Hidalgo3


                        *Corresponding Author, rcurrier@westga.edu
1. University of West Georgia, Department of Natural Sciences, 1601 Maple St., Carrollton, GA, USA, 30118
2. Pennsylvania State University. Department of Geosciences, 116 Deike Building, University Park, PA 16802
 3. Georgia State University, Department of Geosciences, 38 Peachtree Center Ave. SE 7th Floor Suite 730,
                                             Atlanta, GA 30303





This manuscript is a non-peer reviewed preprint submitted to EarthArXiv. This manuscript has been
                   submitted to Contributions in Mineralogy and Petrology





                                                                                  1ABSTRACT
Rock textures observed via thin section are skewed from their true 3D nature. This is due to a variety of
cut effects—artifacts that are introduced due to the lower dimensional nature of the thin section
relative to the rock. Typically, these methods invert crystal shape and crystal size, but with each process
performed separately and in sequence. With the ongoing adoption of electron backscatter diffraction
(EBSD) by petrologists, an additional data stream has now become available: the 3D orientation of 2D
grain sections. For EBSD analysis, no stereological corrections are typically applied for interpreting the
data. In this study, we test whether this orientational information is also skewed due to a fabric cut
effect. We test this by numerically generating synthetic crystal datasets representative of a number of
crystal shapes and population sizes. We find that EBSD orientational data does have a fabric cut effect
since crystals oriented with long axes perpendicular to the thin section are more likely to be sampled
compared to those with long axes oriented parallel to it. This effect needs to be accounted for to
accurately interpret the true 3D fabric. Towards this end, we develop a method of inverting cut fabrics
which provides robust error estimations and show its accuracy using a range of synthetic examples.
When applied to natural samples, which are inherently more complex than the simplified, synthetic
samples, we find that the inversion process does not always produce geologically plausible results. To
more faithfully correct for the different cut effects, we argue that the stereological inversion process
should not be performed separately or sequentially, as is commonly done at present. Instead, we need a
new textural toolkit framework to correct for crystal shape, size, and orientation simultaneously with
accurate uncertainty estimates.

1) Introduction
       Rock texture encapsulates the spatial and geometric characteristics elements within the rock.
Particle shape, size, and orientation are all examples of textural features. The textural information is, in
turn, a critical observational input for characterizing the physical properties of geomaterials and
understanding the processes associated with forming the constituent minerals. For instance, rock
textural features encode many physical properties of the rock, such as seismic wave speed (Satsukawa
et al. 2013; Frothingham et al. 2023), thermal expansivity (Gibert et al. 2003), fluid permeability
(Urumovic and Urumovic 2014), and mechanical strength (Prikryl 2006). Additionally, in igneous rocks,
the mineral grain shape and size are functions of cooling rate (Holness 2014; Mangler et al. 2022;
Marsh,1998), while orientations can encode the kinematic history (e.g. magmatic sense of shear:
Vukmanovic et al. 2018; compaction: Bertolett et al. 2019; Jenkins et al. 2022; grain clustering
mechanisms: Wieser et al. 2019; Holness et al. 2023). Similar applications can be extended into
metamorphic systems with rock fabric encoding the deformation history and behavior (Bernard et al.
2023; Bestmann et al. 2006; Casale et al. 2023; Cross et al. 2017b, Haertel and Herwegh 2014; Fossen
and Cavalcante 2017; Koyama et al. 2023; Levy et al. 2023; Li et al. 2023; Rehman et al. 2023; Taylor et
al. 2023; Wiesman et al. 2023), impact dynamics recorded in meteorites (Goudy et al. 2023; Forman et
al. 2023), fluid reactivity with primary minerals (Andreani et al. 2009; Etschmann et al. 2014; Kang et al.
2010), sedimentary processes (McLaren 1981), as well as biosphere/geosphere interaction
(Hemkemeyer et al. 2018).
         Historically, most textural analyses have been performed in thin section, by measuring the 2D
outlines of the intersection between a crystal and the thin section. This methodology requires little in
terms of instrumentation—a petrographic microscope and illustration software—so the entry cost is
minimal. Over the past few decades, there have been significant improvements - both on the
instrumental side (e.g., digital microscopy, EBSD: electron backscatter diffraction, QEMSCAN:
quantitative evaluation of materials by scanning electron microscopy), as well as data analysis methods
(e.g., image segmentation, shape and spatial analysis), in characterizing the rock microtexture and rapid
processing of large datasets. However, there is still inherently a fundamental challenge with all these





                                                                                   2methods of textural analysis on a thin section: converting 2D in-plane measurements to 3D estimates
using stereological correction techniques. To overcome this challenge, 3D imaging techniques like X-ray
tomography have been developed for textural analysis (Jerram and Higgins 2007; Jerram et al. 2010;
Lanzafame et al. 2017; Polacci et al. 2018). However, these techniques are inherently data intensive
(both in terms of collection and processing), expensive, and are hence not eminently scalable or easily
accessible for the majority of the geoscience community. Thus, 2D thin section analysis remains the
dominant and most accessible form of textural analysis.
      The challenges associated with accurate stereological (2D to 3D) analysis have been known for
decades (Higgins 1994; Howard and Reed 1998; Saltikov 1967; Underwood 1969). Several stereological
2D to 3D correction tools have been developed based on these, especially in the igneous petrology
community (e.g., CSDCorrections: Higgins 2000; CSDslice: Morgan and Jerram 2006; ShapeCalc: Mangler
et al. 2022). The 2D crystal size is by far the most analyzed parameter, corresponding to the areal
intersection of a 3D crystal with the cutting plane of the section. The 3D shape of crystals can be derived
from 2D measurements by adopting different stereological approaches. However, these existing tools
for stereological corrections are based on several simplifying, but hidden, assumptions which may not
be appropriate for each dataset. For instance, analysis methods frequently assume that crystal shape is
constant across all crystal sizes, whereas this can potentially vary across the population (Mock and
Jerram 2005), or as a function of crystal size (Dunbar et al. 1995; Mangler et al. 2022). Analogously, the
tools typically do not provide the full uncertainty covariance matrix between shape, size, and
orientation. In addition, these prepacked tools are typically not fully open source, and without access to
the underlying code for analysis and synthetic crystal cut generation, significant barriers are present for
users to make modifications as needed for their geologic context and datasets.
       There is thus a need for an open source, well-documented, validated, and extendable textural
analysis toolkit for thin section analysis with two key aims: (I) accurate stereological textural corrections,
with associated uncertainties, for shape, size, and orientations, and (II) flexibility to incorporate multiple
types of thin section datasets jointly (i.e. electron beam methodologies as well as different optical
methodologies such as reflected light with different Illumination angles, transmitted light, and cross-
polarized with multiple orientations). The need for this textural toolkit is, in particular, becoming
increasingly relevant since two mature methodologies are capable of automated grain analysis within
the Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM. QEMSCAN utilizes chemical analyses to identify phases, and can
produce grain maps on the basis of these chemical differences. Another technique, EBSD, utilizes crystal
lattice to identify phase and crystal lattice orientation to segment grains (for review, see: Wilkinson and
Britton 2012; Britton et al. 2016). One of the benefits of EBSD analysis is that it can be used for
automated grain segmentation based on the principle of localized orientation clustering within a single
crystal (Cone et al. 2020). Thus, EBSD datasets address some of the key practical challenges with cl

horizontal girdles for the B- and C-axes (and the respective poles to faces (010) and (001)). Because the
crystal morphology and orientations are controlled as input, the connection between crystal shape and
resulting cut fabric can be made, here with the pole perpendicular to the intersection plane coinciding
with the crystal long axis (A = 3), and girdles for the short axes (B = C = 1). From the simple 2D analogy
illustrated in Figure 1d, it is clear that the vertical pole for the A-axis, (100), is due to the higher
probability of intersecting crystals when the long axis is perpendicular to the intersection plane, skewing
the distribution of observed orientations. A simple deduction is that in uniformly distributed
orientations, the cut effect results in a pole along the long axis of the crystal. This is further
demonstrated in Figure 3 with two other crystal shapes (A = 1, B = 3, C = 1, and A = 1, B = 1, C = 3). In
each case, the pole is associated with the long axis of the crystal.
       While the above treatment demonstrates that the cut effect produces artifacts in the ODF for
anisotropic crystal shapes, the results can be made more realistic by taking into consideration the
interaxial angles of the commonly analyzed crystal system of plagioclase (triclinic: e.g., Anorthite, α =
93.166°, β = 115.85°, γ = 91.216°). Plagioclase is the most commonly used phase for textural analyses in
igneous rocks due to its near ubiquity in igneous systems and its wide range of crystallization
temperatures. These interaxial angles are accounted for in the generation of vertices corresponding to
the unrotated crystal. Each crystallographic axis corresponds to a crystallographic face, and so this can
be thought of as an untwinned crystal. Accounting for the interaxial angles slightly modifies the
resultant pole figures (Figure 4). In this case, the crystal shape is: A = 3, B = 1, C = 1. The fabric-cut effect
imposes a vertical pole along the A-axis, (100), a horizontal girdle for the B-axis, (010), and a weaker,
inclined girdle for the C-axis, (001). The inclination of the C-axis girdle is due to the larger interaxial angle
between the A- and C-axes (β = 115.85°). We note that this fabric-cut effect would also persist for non-
uniform ODF scenarios also–except that pole peak and girdle pattern above would be convolved with
the underlying non-uniform orientation distribution.

4.2 Quantifying the Fabric-Cut Effect

strength. The magnitude of this effect can be quantified using a texture index. We utilize the J-index to
quantify the strength of the fabric (Mainprice et al. 2015). J-Index is defined as:

        J-Index ranges from 1 (uniformly distributed) to infinity (single crystal fabric). In the following,
we propose that the J-Index of a sample can be used to measure whether the underlying fabric is

crystal symmetry, and 3) the effect of crystal shape.

## 3. mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 9-11 (Context ID: pqac-00000010)

  INTRODUCTION

Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) is increasingly used to measure two dimensional grain sizes
from sections through engineering materials. The application of the technique can be found in a wide
range of applications and examples are readily found for aluminium alloys [1]; iron and steel [2];
hardmetals [3] and the effects of deformation on grain structure [4]. The technique is capable of
measuring grain size (better than 100 nm) at and below the spatial resolution [5] of current methods
such as optical microscopy.  It also has advantages for providing additional information on the
complex and refined structures that are increasingly required for advanced engineering applications.
The metrological requirements for EBSD and in  particular grain size measurement have been
reviewed [6,7].

There have been several studies comparing the results of grain size measurements by optical and
EBSD methods [1,6,8-12] and for thin films using FIB, AFM microscopies and EBSD [13]. In some
of these works differences were observed in grain size between optical and EBSD and besides the
greater spatial resolution of EBSD technique other factors were implicated, such as limitations of
optical methods in detecting boundaries below a certain misorientation or grain boundary planes  in
optical methods and the variable effectiveness of etching in different samples affecting optical
measurements.

EBSD is used for research and increasingly for quality control, but to fully exploit its potential,
accurate knowledge  is  required  of  the  issues  affecting  the  reproducibility  or  repeatability  of
measurement to enable comparison not only of different EBSD data sets but also comparison with
measurements by other methods.

Some previous comparative data exists on the reproducibility and repeatability of grain sizing by
EBSD for establishing uncertainties associated with the method. An early intercomparison by Randle
[14] et al in 2003 concluded that there was a wide disparity in results between laboratories. A more
comprehensive Round Robin [15] looking at various aspects of EBSD was performed on 7 different
materials, delivered by Nordic metal producing companies and investigated by up to 9 laboratories.
Four of the laboratories acquitted themselves well. The author concluded that EBSD can do a very
good job on very difficult materials, but the success depends on :
     Resolution of the SEM
     Type of EBSD-camera.
     Specimen preparation
     Operator skill
As a result a meeting was arranged to improve the quality of measurement in November 2004. The
author of this report stated recently that in her opinion [16] the development of equipment and
expertise since 2004 made a new round robin exercise appropriate.

This present report contains results from a preliminary interlaboratory comparison carried out to
measure the grain  size by EBSD  in a titanium metal sample with an average grain  size of
approximately 30 µm. The sample is also amenable to optical microscopy methods of grain size
measurement such as ASTM E112 [17]. This work is part supported by VAMAS TWA 37 Project 1
with the objective to validate the proposed International Standard, ISO/DIS ISO13067 “Microbeam
analysis-Electron Backscatter Diffraction-Measurement of Grain Size and Distribution” prepared by
ISO TC202/WG7.

To enable a round robin to be carried out in a reasonable timescale, multiple samples were prepared
from a single source for distribution to participants rather than sending one sample on from laboratory
to laboratory.  While the latter route might be preferable, in theory enabling a better comparison
between  laboratories by  eliminating sample  to sample  variability,  in  practice  variable sample
contamination from each EBSD mapping run accumulating with each analysis and handling damage



                                     3                                            NPL Report MAT 56


would require regular sample repreparation, negating the benefit of a single sample as well as
substantially slowing down the time to obtain results.
The laboratories participating in the round robin represented:
                    3 EBSD equipment manufacturers
                    5 National Measurement Institutes (NMIs)
                    1 university
                    2 industrial research laboratories
They also represented a wide geographical spread, coming from 8 countries: France; Germany;
Sweden; UK; USA; South Africa; China and Brazil.

The main body of this report presents a summary of the results and discusses reasons for the observed
variability of results in detail including:
                     Magnification errors
                     Orthogonality of scan
                     Step size
                     Specification of minimum grain size
                     Clean up of map noise

2.1   SAMPLE PREPARATION

Samples were cut using electrodischarge machining from a 15 mm diameter bar of commercial purity
titanium to provide 2 mm thick slices.  The slices were not kept in sequence and were randomly
assigned an identifying number. To enable polishing of multiple samples the slices were hot-mounted
in bakelite and then ground and polished by a conventional mechanical polishing route but finishing
with a combined chemical-mechanical stage using colloidal silica diluted with 20% H2O2.  The
samples were marked with a hardness indent at one point on the edge and one at the approximate
centre of the sample to assist with identification of positions where measurements were made.

that a better indication of the homogeneity of the samples was subsequently obtained from the larger
amounts of data produced by all the participants.

2.6  EBSD map step size and grain boundary threshold angle

Grain size is intrinsically linked to the EBSD map step size and boundary threshold

angle in typical AM microstructures, which have large intragranular rotations and sub-

grain boundary structures. The distinction between grain boundaries and sub-grain

boundaries is somewhat arbitrary and depends on the grain boundary threshold angle

value, as well as the grain reconstruction method. The EBSD map step size affects the

effective grain boundary threshold angle during grain reconstruction, because grainboundaries are defined by the misorientation angle between adjacent points. When the

step size is extremely large, grains can also be broken up because pixel-connectivity is

lost in the thin regions of non-convex grains.

A longer step size decreases the measured grain size, because grain boundaries with

misorientation just above the threshold angle at a larger step size are no longer classified

as grain boundaries at a smaller step size, since the same misorientation is split between

more map points. Figure 5 shows an example of this: the EBSD map (a) was 2 × 2

1. Introduction
Electron diffraction offers an opportunity to study the internal structure of materials. In the scanning
electron microscope (SEM), we can perform electron diffraction using backscattering electrons.
   In electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), these electrons enter the sample and scatter through
electron-matter interactions [1]. If the sample is tilted to a high angle, a high fraction of these scattering
electrons escape, and if their last scattering angle is favourably oriented with respect to the crystal lattice
they will diffract according to Bragg’s law [2]. In the kinematic approximation of diffraction, edges to
Kikuchi bands are formed at an angle ± θ with respect to the perpendicular of the plane normal of the
diffracting plane [3]. The EBSD pattern contains many bands, which are located on the phosphor screen
as a function of the microscope settings (i.e., voltage), crystal orientation, lattice parameters, and the
location of the imaging screen (i.e., the pattern centre) [4]. The geometry of the electron scattering
process results in the formation of a direct projection of the diffracting lattice planes.
  A change in band width (e.g., due to a change in a hydrostatic strain state) can occur due to the
change in interplanar spacing affecting Bragg’s law but the conventional EBSD geometry is relatively
insensitive to this [5]. A change in interplanar angles will cause the bands to move across the diffracting
pattern and this is more obvious and therefore measurable. For a deformation experiment, these changes
can be induced by the presence of a (relative) deviatoric strain, and furthermore the bands may move
across the screen due to the crystal rotating due to the presence and movement of dislocations during
crystal slip. The presence of stored dislocations which result in local orientation gradients, can be linked
through Nye’s analysis [6] and therefore high precision measurements of spatial rotation gradients can
be used to estimate the lower bound of the stored dislocation content [7, 8].

Conventional, Hough based, EBSD uses band identification, through peak identification in Hough
space, and subsequent indexing to identify the crystal orientation [4]. Work by Humphrey’s indicates
that the effective precision of this approach for misorientation analysis is ~ 0.5° (i.e., 0.0087 rads) [14].
The high resolution EBSD analysis, introduced principally by Wilkinson, Meaden and Dingley [7, 8] in
2006 directly compares the two diffraction patterns using cross correlation based image analysis to
precisely measure the change in interplanar angles and results in an increase in measurement precision
of two orders of magnitude, i.e., 0.0001 rads [7, 8].
These subtle shifts can be ascribed to lattice deformations resulting from a change in the lattice
parameters due to a deviatoric change in lattice strain and therefore enable, using Hooke’s law and a
plane stress assumption, the residual stress variations between points within a single grain to be
evaluated with a precision of ~20 MPa (for a material with a Young’s modulus of 200 GPa).
  The HR-EBSD technique has been widely applied across a range of semiconductor [7, 15],
superconductor [16, 17], metals (e.g., [18-20]) and geological systems [21], often within the scope of
understanding local changes in lattice parameter and especially within the field of deformation analysis.
   In this manuscript, we will briefly introduce the key methodology of the technique. This will be
followed by an example showing its efficacy at resolving high resolution orientation gradients in
deformed copper and focus on studying the storage of geometrically necessary dislocations around an
indent made in interstitial free (IF) steel.

2. Methodology
HR-EBSD involves analysis of diffraction patterns that are captured using the conventional EBSD set-
up, with the camera inserted as for a texture or grain mapping experiment. The only differences are that
the quality of the sample preparation must be higher (as surface scratches or deformation is more evident
when the precision of the experiment is higher) and that the best quality patterns are captured. The

within 5 pixels [24] and typical optical distortions are reasonable [24].

  The reference pattern is sub-divided into many ‘regions of interest’ (ROI), which for a 1,000 x 1,000
pixel image are often 256 x 256 pixels in size [8] and this is repeated for a test pattern, extracted for a
point within the same grain. At each ROI, the pattern is extracted and transferred to the Fourier domain
for filtering and frequency based cross-correlation.  The FFT based cross-correlation enables rapid
calculation of the best translation vector between test and reference ROIs.  If the translation of four or
more well-spaced ROIs are measured well, then with knowledge of the pattern centre, eight components
of the deformation tensor can be extracted. For the impact of strain and lattice rotation on the pattern,
see Fig. 1. The ninth of deformation is the hydrostatic strain, which can be calculated only using an out
of plane stress traction free boundary condition and Hooke’s law.
   Reasonable measurement of the translation shift is achieved using sub-pixel precision through up-
sampling techniques (i.e., the centre of the cross-correlation peak is determined with sub-pixel accuracy
as we assume that the shape of the peak is smooth – see [26] for more information).
  Mapping strain and rotation within a map requires capturing of two patterns with the same geometry.
Typically, EBSD maps are capturing using ‘beam scanning’ approaches where the electron beam is
deflected and rastered across the sample. If the sample is flat and well aligned in the microscope (i.e.
the sample plane normal is well known) then it is possible to construct a simple geometrical model
where the beam shift can be corrected for (this is trivially accounted for in commercial software). This
correction is important when the beam is shifted by a similar amplitude to the pattern shifts which arise
due to strain or lattice rotation. Modern indirect detectors have a effective pixel size of ~20-40 µm, and
therefore a uncertainties of in the prediction of the beam shift of 1 µm can result in systematic errors in
the calculation of deformation tensors. Alignment of the sample can be assisted greatly through careful
insertion into the SEM and presentation with respect to the beam, for instance using special sample
holders (for example see page 85, chapter 2.3.3.2 of reference [27]). Note that for GND analysis (on
which this paper focusses), beam shift errors have a less significant role as GNDs are calculated using
local gradients between neighbour points).
   Recently, it has been shown by both Maurice et al. [28] and Britton and Wilkinson [25] that the
presence of a significant rotation gradient between test and reference pattern results in significant
inaccuracy in the measurement of elastic strain, e.g., for metallic systems. Therefore, the algorithm has
recently been updated to include a remapping step [25], whereby the pattern intensities of one pattern
are remapped to better match the orientation of the other prior to extracting the strain components. The
total contribution of the remapping and the shift measurements are combined to extract the deformation
gradient tensor.
  The deformation gradient tensor can be split into strain and rotation using either a finite or
infinitesimal decomposition framework. In the case of small strains and small rotations these two are
approximately equivalent, and for HR-EBSD, the finite framework is typically used for cases of large
lattice rotation differences (as the strain gradients are typically small, due to the elastic limit in most
materials).
  The HR-EBSD pattern matching approach provides the best ‘guess’ to fit a model that maps the
intensities of one pattern onto another, and this model is used to calculate the deformation gradient (see
Fig. 2).  This approach has been validated extensively using both experimental comparisons, e.g.,
through comparisons with NIST traceable Raman based stress measurements and AFM in Si [29, 30],
comparison with modelling [15, 23, 32], comparison with X-ray based micro-Laue diffraction [32], and
algorithm validation using dynamically simulated diffraction patterns [15, 22, 23].

  One particular aspect of this work has been the generation of ‘quality’ metrics [26] that indicate when
the HR-EBSD method fails. The mean angular error (MAE) describes the difference between the pattern
shifts as measured and the predicted pattern shifts per the model, and a high value (i.e., greater than the
measurement made) indicates the precision, and not accuracy, obtained. The (normalised) peak height
describes the degree of matching for the cross-correlation peak, and it is often formatted as a geometric
mean of all ROI peak heights normalised against auto correlation. Measurements using simulations
have indicated that when this value falls below 0.3, the measurement is unlikely to be reasonable [32].
These two metrics can be used to rapidly screen data from large maps to remove suspect points, however
further care must be taken when reporting stress variations (for example) as for example, not using a
remapping step can result in artificially high stresses to be reported which are not physically reasonable
[33].
  Once the lattice rotations between test and reference are measured, it is possible to utilise Nye’s
framework [6] to estimate the geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density and this has proved a
very popular aspect of the technique [12, 13, 19, 34, 35]. In short, for each point within the orientation
gradient map, a local gradient of the lattice rotation field is calculated and use to determine the lattice
curvature (the adaptive kernel we use is described in [36]). As three rotation terms are measured in a
2D map, six components of lattice curvature are calculated. From Nye’s formulation, the presence of
GNDs can support these lattice curvatures, and it is a ‘simple’ task of solving the following equation for
ρ:

   where ρ are the curvature types, Λ are lattice curvatures, and ξ is the outer product of the Burgers
vector and line direction for each dislocation type (the origin of this equation and its use for HR-EBSD
measurements is explained in Wilkinson and Randman [12]).
   For a metallic system, such as for FCC crystals such as Cu, the equation is underdetermined as there
are many more potential dislocation types (12 {111} <110> edge, and 6 <110> screw [37]) than
constraints from measurement of lattice curvature and therefore following the work of Wilkinson and
Randman [12], we have chosen to find a potential solution that reduces the self-energy of the
dislocations (accounting for screw and edge types, as well as changes in Burgers vector length) in a so
called “L-1 minimisation” formulation.  This solution is one of many solutions to the problem that
necessarily supports the lattice curvature, but it may not be unique.

| Hough indexing / conventional EBSD vs HR-EBSD precision | Misorientation, KAM-like local rotation metrics, GND density floor | Conventional Hough-based EBSD: absolute orientation ~2°; misorientation precision ~0.1–0.5°. HR-EBSD: relative misorientation precision ~0.006° (1×10^-4 rad), i.e. about two orders of magnitude better. Estimated measurable GND lower bounds at 1 μm step are >3×10^13 m^-2 for conventional EBSD versus >3×10^11 m^-2 for HR-EBSD; at 100 nm step, >3×10^14 versus >3×10^12 m^-2 (pqac-00000013) | Better angular precision lowers the noise floor on local misorientation and thus on GND estimates derived from orientation gradients; conventional Hough indexing can substantially overstate the floor and blur subtle orientation gradients (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014) | Report indexing/analysis method when presenting KAM/GND-like quantities; results from conventional EBSD and HR-EBSD are not directly comparable without noting their very different angular precision and GND detection floor (pqac-00000013) |
| Texture sample size and cut-section bias | Texture strength, ODF/J-index | For synthetic cut fabrics, the cut effect increased texture strength above the true uniform value; with increasing sample size, J-index decreases and asymptotically converges, with minimal further change beyond ~2000 crystal orientations sampled. Example ODFs with n = 3000 still showed cut-induced fabric from a truly uniform ODF (pqac-00000009) | Thin-section/2D EBSD sampling preferentially intersects elongated crystals when their long axis is closer to section normal, creating a systematic, non-random ODF bias and inflating apparent texture strength (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) | Report sample size for texture analysis and recognize that 2D EBSD ODFs can have morphology-driven cut bias; community calls for joint stereological correction of shape, size, and orientation with uncertainty estimates (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) |
| 3D GBCD alignment, out-of-plane spacing, and discretization | GBCD peak intensities, coherent twin fraction, GBED | For Σ3 in Ni, 3D GBCD peak at the coherent twin plane was 240 MRD with 1:1 spacing and no secondary alignment; 390 MRD with 2:1 spacing; 670 MRD with secondary alignment at 1:1; and 1090 MRD with both 2:1 spacing and secondary alignment, essentially matching the stereological result of 1100 MRD (pqac-00000016). Changing discretization from 9 to 11 bins per 90° increased the twin population to 3600 MRD because the ideal twin no longer lay on a bin boundary (pqac-00000016) | GBCD is highly sensitive to layer alignment, voxel aspect ratio, and binning/discretization; poor alignment suppresses sharp special-boundary peaks, while discretization choices can create large apparent intensity changes (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016) | For GBCD/GBED, report alignment procedure, out-of-plane:in-plane spacing, matching tolerances (<5° used for triple-junction matching), and discretization scheme; otherwise special-boundary populations are not reproducible (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016) |
| SEM tilt and drift / geometric distortion | Grain size, especially area-based metrics; boundary geometry | In Ti reanalysis, adding 2° tilt caused a grain-size reduction factor of 0.95 from cos(72°)/cos(70°) (pqac-00000011). In 2026 synthetic distortion work, most methods stayed within ΔG ±0.5 ASTM grain-size numbers under typical conditions; intercept methods were more sensitive, reaching up to about ±2 G under drift, planimetric methods changed by ~1 G, and TPC/ASTM E2627 was least sensitive (pqac-00000004) | Tilt error foreshortens the mapped y direction and biases area-based size downward; drift elongates/distorts grains, with stronger impact on intercept-based metrics than on robust planimetric/TPC approaches (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000004) | Report specimen tilt calibration, scan orthogonality/stability, and any distortion correction; if possible compare x and y intercepts to diagnose tilt/drift asymmetry (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) |
| Interlaboratory / inter-software reproducibility | Grain size and uncertainty budgets | In the 12-lab Ti round robin, 4 of 12 laboratories gave significantly different grain-size results; after outlier removal, reproducibility standard deviation was 1.98 μm for equivalent circle diameter and 1.15 μm for linear intercept, and equivalent-circle values were ~10% higher than linear intercept. Reproducibility limit for Dcircle was 70% greater than for Dlin (Rcircle = 5.79, Rlin = 3.36) (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011). AM work concludes combined expanded uncertainty k = 2 of about 20% is achievable when step size, threshold, cleanup, and sampling are controlled (pqac-00000003) | Major between-lab discrepancies came from magnification calibration, step size, minimum grain cutoff, cleanup, tilt, and insufficient mapped area. Area-based metrics were more sensitive than intercept metrics to geometric/calibration errors (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000010) | Reproducible EBSD grain size requires reporting acquisition geometry, calibration, step size, threshold angle, cutoff, cleanup, map size/FoV, and statistic used; standards-oriented workflows can achieve ~20% expanded uncertainty, but operator choices otherwise dominate (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000010) |

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab

drug_names.description:
