answer.answer:
# Sensitivity, uncertainty, and reproducibility of EBSD-derived microstructural measurements

## Executive conclusion

EBSD-derived quantities are **not intrinsic outputs of the orientation map alone**. Grain size/count, low-angle versus high-angle boundary fractions, KAM/GND, texture strength, and GBCD are conditional on spatial sampling, orientation precision, indexing, reconstruction, cleanup, censoring, and statistical weighting. The strongest quantitative evidence concerns grain size: plausible operator and software choices can change number-weighted results by **±26–100%**, while carefully constructed area-weighted measures typically vary by **±0.2–10%**. A standards-oriented workflow can achieve a combined expanded uncertainty of roughly **20% at k=2**, but uncontrolled workflows can differ far more. Formal uncertainty studies are substantially less mature for KAM/GND, LAGB/HAGB fractions, texture intensity, and GBCD. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24)

The evidence-supported parameter effects are summarized below.

| Parameter / operation | Affected outputs | Quantified literature result | Direction / mechanism of bias | Reporting / best-practice implication |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EBSD step size | Grain size, grain count, reconstructed connectivity | ISO 13067 recommends step size ≈ 10% of average grain diameter; AM study argues 20% can be too coarse for non-convex grains. In a Hastelloy-X example, binning from 3 μm to 6 μm reduced maximum grain size from 1250 μm to 970 μm, and median plus 75th-percentile minimum Feret diameter decreased systematically as step size increased from 1.25 to 15 μm (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 16-20, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16) | Larger step size can split thin/non-convex grains by loss of pixel connectivity and changes the effective boundary threshold because misorientation is measured only between adjacent points; reported effect in AM microstructures was a systematic decrease in measured grain size with coarser step size (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16) | Always report step size together with grain-boundary threshold angle; comparisons are invalid unless both are identical, especially where subgrain structure or intragranular rotations are present (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 16-20, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24) |
| Grain-boundary misorientation threshold for reconstruction | Grain size, grain count, LAGB/HAGB fractions | In the Ti round robin reanalysis table, using 15° instead of 5° increased measured grain size from 30.5 to 31.8 μm at 0.5 μm step with 2 μm cutoff (+4.3%), from 35.9 to 37.5 μm at 3 μm step with 10 μm cutoff (+4.5%), from 34.9 to 36.9 μm at 3 μm +2° tilt (+5.7%), and from 33.6 to 35.4 μm in another 3 μm condition (+5.4%) (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26). AM guidance recommends 10° rather than 5° when subgrain structure is present (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 1-5) | Raising the threshold merges more low-angle boundaries into grains, increasing grain size and reducing counted grain number; it also directly shifts LAGB/HAGB fractions because the class boundary is user-defined (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16) | Must report the exact threshold angle used for grain reconstruction and any distinction between grain and subgrain boundaries (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26) |
| Minimum-grain-size cutoff | Grain size, grain count, size distribution | Standards cited in AM study exclude grains below 10 points (ISO 13067) or 100 points (ASTM E2627). The Ti round robin identified smallest-grain cutoff as the main source of interlaboratory variation; small grains had a disproportionate effect on averages (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 1-9). In one AM example, only 0.6% of indexed points belonged to grains <10 points, but excluding them still had to be accounted for in cumulative histograms (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16) | Removing small grains systematically inflates reported grain size and lowers grain count; effect is strongest for number-weighted statistics and for maps with non-random unindexed boundary pixels (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 16-20, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 1-9) | Report the cutoff in both pixels/points and micrometres, plus the indexed area fraction removed by the cutoff (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24) |
| Indexing fraction, CI/fit thresholding, and cleanup extent | Grain size, grain count, reproducibility | Grain-cleanup uncertainty was ±13% for maps with 65% indexing versus ±4% for maps with 95% indexing (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 16-20). In AM inter-software comparisons, number-weighted grain-size metrics varied by ±26–100% with different clean-up methods, while area-weighted metrics varied by only ±0.2–10% (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10). One round robin noted acceptable indexing around ~80%, despite a nominal 95% target (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32) | Unindexed points are not spatially random; they cluster near boundaries and especially distort small grains, causing artificial fragmentation or linking. Cleanup that reassigns low-confidence points can materially change grain topology (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 16-20, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 1-5, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26) | Report indexed fraction, CI/fit thresholds, whether low-confidence pixels were removed or reassigned, and the difference between no cleanup and maximum cleanup if used for uncertainty estimation (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26) |
| Cleanup operations such as grain dilation / reassignment | Grain size, grain count, boundary network, potentially boundary fractions | In 3D GBCD work, data were cleaned with two iterations of grain dilation and a minimum grain size of 10 pixels; groups of <10 pixels with disorientations <5° were reassigned to adjacent grains (rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 2-4). AM grain-size work notes standards constraints that cleanup should change results by ≤5% (ISO 13067) or ≤10% (ASTM E2627) (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10) | These operations systematically erase small grains and smooth/regularize boundaries, tending to increase grain size and reduce grain count unless tightly constrained; they also alter the boundary network used for downstream boundary statistics (rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 2-4, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10) | Cleanup routines should be constrained by standards limits and described explicitly, including iterations and reassignment rules (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10, rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 2-4) |
| Area-weighted vs number-weighted statistics; edge-grain exclusion | Average grain size, histogram quantiles, reproducibility | Number-weighted metrics changed by ±26–100% across cleanup methods, versus ±0.2–10% for area-weighted metrics (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10). In one AM dataset, indexed-area-weighted median uncertainty half-range was ±1.5% for MFD (207 μm) and ±9.3% for grain area (6290 μm²), whereas conventional area-weighted medians showed ±16% for MFD (179 μm) and ±33% for grain area (4875 μm²) because of field-size and threshold sensitivity (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16) | Number weighting overemphasizes numerous small grains and is highly sensitive to cleanup/cutoff choices. Excluding edge grains without correction underestimates area-weighted grain size when map size is small relative to grain size (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16) | Prefer indexed-area-weighted median MFD; exclude edge grains but document the excluded area fraction and consider Miles-Lantejoul correction where applicable (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16) |
| Hough indexing / conventional EBSD vs HR-EBSD precision | Misorientation, KAM-like local rotation metrics, GND density floor | Conventional Hough-based EBSD: absolute orientation ~2°; misorientation precision ~0.1–0.5°. HR-EBSD: relative misorientation precision ~0.006° (1×10^-4 rad), i.e. about two orders of magnitude better. Estimated measurable GND lower bounds at 1 μm step are >3×10^13 m^-2 for conventional EBSD versus >3×10^11 m^-2 for HR-EBSD; at 100 nm step, >3×10^14 versus >3×10^12 m^-2 (britton2018understandingdeformationwith pages 1-3) | Better angular precision lowers the noise floor on local misorientation and thus on GND estimates derived from orientation gradients; conventional Hough indexing can substantially overstate the floor and blur subtle orientation gradients (britton2018understandingdeformationwith pages 1-3, britton2018understandingdeformationwith pages 3-6) | Report indexing/analysis method when presenting KAM/GND-like quantities; results from conventional EBSD and HR-EBSD are not directly comparable without noting their very different angular precision and GND detection floor (britton2018understandingdeformationwith pages 1-3) |
| Texture sample size and cut-section bias | Texture strength, ODF/J-index | For synthetic cut fabrics, the cut effect increased texture strength above the true uniform value; with increasing sample size, J-index decreases and asymptotically converges, with minimal further change beyond ~2000 crystal orientations sampled. Example ODFs with n = 3000 still showed cut-induced fabric from a truly uniform ODF (currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 9-12) | Thin-section/2D EBSD sampling preferentially intersects elongated crystals when their long axis is closer to section normal, creating a systematic, non-random ODF bias and inflating apparent texture strength (currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 1-3, currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 9-12) | Report sample size for texture analysis and recognize that 2D EBSD ODFs can have morphology-driven cut bias; community calls for joint stereological correction of shape, size, and orientation with uncertainty estimates (currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 1-3, currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 9-12) |
| 3D GBCD alignment, out-of-plane spacing, and discretization | GBCD peak intensities, coherent twin fraction, GBED | For Σ3 in Ni, 3D GBCD peak at the coherent twin plane was 240 MRD with 1:1 spacing and no secondary alignment; 390 MRD with 2:1 spacing; 670 MRD with secondary alignment at 1:1; and 1090 MRD with both 2:1 spacing and secondary alignment, essentially matching the stereological result of 1100 MRD (rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 4-5). Changing discretization from 9 to 11 bins per 90° increased the twin population to 3600 MRD because the ideal twin no longer lay on a bin boundary (rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 4-5) | GBCD is highly sensitive to layer alignment, voxel aspect ratio, and binning/discretization; poor alignment suppresses sharp special-boundary peaks, while discretization choices can create large apparent intensity changes (rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 2-4, rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 4-5) | For GBCD/GBED, report alignment procedure, out-of-plane:in-plane spacing, matching tolerances (<5° used for triple-junction matching), and discretization scheme; otherwise special-boundary populations are not reproducible (rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 2-4, rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 4-5) |
| SEM tilt and drift / geometric distortion | Grain size, especially area-based metrics; boundary geometry | In Ti reanalysis, adding 2° tilt caused a grain-size reduction factor of 0.95 from cos(72°)/cos(70°) (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26). In 2026 synthetic distortion work, most methods stayed within ΔG ±0.5 ASTM grain-size numbers under typical conditions; intercept methods were more sensitive, reaching up to about ±2 G under drift, planimetric methods changed by ~1 G, and TPC/ASTM E2627 was least sensitive (timberlake2026effectsofsem pages 14-17) | Tilt error foreshortens the mapped y direction and biases area-based size downward; drift elongates/distorts grains, with stronger impact on intercept-based metrics than on robust planimetric/TPC approaches (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26, timberlake2026effectsofsem pages 14-17) | Report specimen tilt calibration, scan orthogonality/stability, and any distortion correction; if possible compare x and y intercepts to diagnose tilt/drift asymmetry (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 9-11, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26) |
| Interlaboratory / inter-software reproducibility | Grain size and uncertainty budgets | In the 12-lab Ti round robin, 4 of 12 laboratories gave significantly different grain-size results; after outlier removal, reproducibility standard deviation was 1.98 μm for equivalent circle diameter and 1.15 μm for linear intercept, and equivalent-circle values were ~10% higher than linear intercept. Reproducibility limit for Dcircle was 70% greater than for Dlin (Rcircle = 5.79, Rlin = 3.36) (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 1-9, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26). AM work concludes combined expanded uncertainty k = 2 of about 20% is achievable when step size, threshold, cleanup, and sampling are controlled (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24) | Major between-lab discrepancies came from magnification calibration, step size, minimum grain cutoff, cleanup, tilt, and insufficient mapped area. Area-based metrics were more sensitive than intercept metrics to geometric/calibration errors (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 1-9, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 9-11) | Reproducible EBSD grain size requires reporting acquisition geometry, calibration, step size, threshold angle, cutoff, cleanup, map size/FoV, and statistic used; standards-oriented workflows can achieve ~20% expanded uncertainty, but operator choices otherwise dominate (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 9-11) |


*Table: This table summarizes quantitative literature evidence on how key EBSD acquisition and post-processing choices change grain size, texture, boundary statistics, and orientation-gradient metrics. It is useful as a compact checklist of known sensitivities, systematic biases, and reporting requirements needed for reproducible EBSD analysis.*

## 1. Quantified sensitivity studies

### 1.1 Step size and mapped area

Step size affects both spatial resolution and the *effective* grain-reconstruction criterion. In microstructures with smooth intragranular rotation, the same total rotation is divided among more neighboring points at fine step size; coarsening can therefore make point-to-point misorientation exceed the reconstruction threshold and split a formerly connected grain. Coarse sampling can also disconnect narrow regions of non-convex grains. In an AM Hastelloy-X example, increasing step size from **3 to 6 μm** reduced the maximum reconstructed minimum-Feret diameter from **1250 to 970 μm**. Binning from **1.25 to 15 μm** produced a systematic decline in median and 75th-percentile minimum-Feret diameter. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16)

ISO 13067-oriented guidance is approximately **one step per 10% of mean grain diameter**. A commonly used 20%-of-diameter rule can be inadequate for non-convex AM grains. Step size and boundary threshold are interdependent and must be held fixed for comparisons. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 16-20, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24)

Field of view is at least as important as pixel density. Bootstrap analysis found approximately **10% sampling uncertainty at a field width of 15 grain lengths**, with the mean stabilizing above roughly seven grain lengths but outlier risk remaining. The proposed robust condition is about **20 grain lengths per field of view**, especially for elongated AM grains. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16)

### 1.2 Grain-reconstruction misorientation tolerance

Increasing the reconstruction threshold merges boundaries and therefore increases mean grain size and decreases grain count. In the titanium round-robin reanalysis, changing the boundary threshold from **5° to 15°** increased mean size:

- **30.5 to 31.8 μm** at 0.5 μm step and 2 μm cutoff: **+4.3%**;
- **35.9 to 37.5 μm** at 3 μm step and 10 μm cutoff: **+4.5%**;
- **34.9 to 36.9 μm** in a tilted condition: **+5.7%**;
- **33.6 to 35.4 μm** in another 3 μm condition: **+5.4%**. (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26)

This parameter also directly determines LAGB/HAGB fractions: raising the grain threshold reclassifies or removes boundaries in the interval between the old and new thresholds. Thus a reported “LAGB fraction” is uninterpretable unless the lower noise cutoff, LAGB/HAGB dividing angle, reconstruction rule, and length/segment weighting are stated. For AM structures containing intragranular rotations, 10° has been recommended over 5° for identifying morphological grains, but that is a purpose-dependent convention rather than a universal physical boundary. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 1-5, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16)

### 1.3 Minimum-grain cutoff and grain weighting

The minimum accepted grain size was the **largest identified source of interlaboratory variation** in the titanium round robin. Small grains disproportionately affect number-weighted means, and the effect depends on step size, indexing quality, and treatment of unindexed points. ISO 13067 and ASTM E2627 were reported as using markedly different exclusion scales—approximately **10 points** and **100 points**, respectively—so “standard-compliant” analyses can still differ unless the standard and implementation are specified. Cutoffs should be reported in both pixels and physical units. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 1-9)

The direction of bias is systematic: removing small grains lowers grain count and raises number-weighted mean grain size. In inter-software AM analyses, changing cleanup produced **±26–100%** changes in number-weighted metrics but only **±0.2–10%** in area-weighted metrics. Indexed-area-weighted median minimum-Feret diameter is consequently much more robust than a number mean. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10)

In one AM dataset, indexed-area-weighted medians had half-ranges of only **±1.5% for MFD** and **±9.3% for grain area**. Conventional area-weighted medians varied by **±16%** and **±33%**, respectively, because field-size, edge, and cutoff effects were not fully represented. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16)

### 1.4 Indexing fraction, confidence/fit thresholds, and cleanup

Cleanup sensitivity rises sharply as raw map quality declines. Estimated cleanup uncertainty was **±13% at 65% indexing**, compared with **±4% at 95% indexing**. Unindexed points are generally not missing at random; they concentrate at boundaries, deformed areas, fine features, and weak patterns. Depending on topology, they can fragment one grain into several or allow adjacent grains to be linked after filling. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 16-20)

The titanium round robin compared systems that either indexed every point with a confidence measure or left points unindexed when fit criteria failed. One reanalysis rendered points with **confidence index <0.1** unindexed. This illustrates why “indexing percentage” cannot be compared independently of the CI or fit threshold and indexing philosophy. Approximately 80% indexing was workable in that particular round robin despite a nominal 95% target, but it was not evidence that 80% is generally sufficient. (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26)

Grain dilation is explicitly topology-changing. One 3D GBCD workflow used **two iterations**, a **10-pixel minimum grain**, and reassigned groups below 10 pixels whose disorientation was below **5°** to an adjacent grain. Such processing erases small components and modifies boundary geometry; it is not neutral denoising. (rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 2-4)

The standards-oriented limits reported in the AM study were that cleanup should alter results by no more than **5% under ISO 13067** or **10% under ASTM E2627**. These limits should be treated as acceptance checks, not proof that the cleaned map is unbiased. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10)

Direct controlled, transferable numerical studies for **neighbor orientation correlation, neighbor pattern averaging, and vendor-specific CI standardization** were not found in the retrieved quantitative literature. Their expected directions are nevertheless clear: orientation-correlation filling and dilation remove isolated grains and shorten or move boundaries; neighbor-pattern averaging improves signal-to-noise but mixes patterns across boundaries unless boundary-aware, degrading spatial resolution and potentially suppressing narrow grains and LAGBs. Because the magnitude is dataset- and implementation-specific, it should be measured by raw-versus-processed parameter sweeps rather than assumed.

### 1.5 Indexing method and orientation precision: Hough, refinement, and HR-EBSD

Conventional Hough EBSD has reported absolute-orientation accuracy of roughly **2°** and relative misorientation precision of approximately **0.1–0.5°**. Cross-correlation HR-EBSD reaches about **0.006°**, an improvement of roughly two orders of magnitude. This difference changes the noise floor of every local-misorientation-derived quantity. (britton2018understandingdeformationwith pages 1-3)

For Burgers vector magnitude 0.3 nm, estimated measurable GND floors at **1 μm step** are above approximately **3×10¹³ m⁻²** for conventional Hough EBSD and **3×10¹¹ m⁻²** for HR-EBSD. At **100 nm step**, the corresponding floors rise to **3×10¹⁴** and **3×10¹² m⁻²** because curvature divides angular error by spatial separation. (britton2018understandingdeformationwith pages 1-3)

HR-EBSD also has analysis choices: reference and test patterns should remain within roughly **12°** for adequate overlap; normalized cross-correlation peak height below **0.3** indicates an unreliable result in simulations; and omitting rotational remapping can generate artificially high stresses. GND inversion is underdetermined and produces a lower-bound solution conditional on the selected dislocation types and optimization norm. (britton2018understandingdeformationwith pages 3-6)

The retrieved full-text evidence did not support a defensible universal numerical conversion between **Hough, dictionary indexing, and full-pattern orientation refinement** for grain size, texture intensity, or GBCD. The robust conclusion is narrower: full-pattern/cross-correlation refinement greatly reduces relative angular noise and therefore materially changes KAM/GND and near-threshold LAGB statistics, whereas grain topology will change mainly where Hough misindexing or angular error lies near the chosen reconstruction threshold. Method, pattern resolution/binning, refinement model, and quality rejection threshold must therefore be reported.

### 1.6 KAM and GND density

KAM is particularly parameter-dependent because it is an average over a user-defined neighborhood, normally after rejecting neighbor pairs above a chosen angle. Changing step size changes the physical kernel radius; changing neighbor order changes spatial smoothing; changing the exclusion angle changes whether boundaries and subboundaries enter the calculation; cleanup suppresses isolated angular outliers and therefore usually lowers KAM. GND density additionally scales as orientation gradient, approximately angular change divided by step length, so its noise floor rises as step size decreases unless angular precision improves proportionally. The Hough-versus-HR floors above quantify this effect. (britton2018understandingdeformationwith pages 1-3)

Consequently, KAM or GND values are not reproducible if only “KAM was calculated” is reported. Required information includes step size, neighbor shell/kernel and physical radius, boundary exclusion angle, whether zero/unindexed neighbors are omitted, indexing/refinement method and angular precision, smoothing or cleanup, Burgers vector, finite-difference scheme, assumed slip/dislocation systems, inversion norm, and whether the value is a lower bound. The retrieved corpus contained no mature interlaboratory uncertainty standard for KAM/GND comparable to ASTM E2627 or ISO 13067 for grain size.

### 1.7 Texture strength and ODF intensity

Texture has two separable sensitivities: orientation-measurement error and statistical/sectioning bias. Synthetic sectioning showed that even a truly uniform 3D ODF can acquire a nonuniform 2D EBSD ODF because elongated grains are more likely to be intersected when their long axes are near the section normal. This systematically inflates apparent fabric strength; it is not random angular noise. (currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 1-3, currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 9-12)

For repeated synthetic trials, the J-index decreased toward its asymptote as grain count increased; above approximately **2000 crystal orientations**, further sample-size effect was minimal. ODFs based on **3000 grains** could nevertheless retain morphology-driven cut bias. Kernel optimization also generated small “stair-step” changes in J-index as sample size changed, demonstrating that ODF bandwidth is itself a processing parameter. (currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 9-12)

Thus texture reporting should specify whether orientations are point-, grain-, or area-weighted; number of independent grains and points; ODF kernel/bandwidth and symmetry; section orientation; grain-shape anisotropy; and any smoothing or removal of low-quality points. Point weighting overrepresents large grains, while one-orientation-per-grain weighting gives each grain equal weight. Neither is universally correct; the estimand must be declared.

### 1.8 Boundary fractions and GBCD

LAGB/HAGB fractions are highly sensitive near both the angular-resolution floor and the chosen class boundary. Conventional Hough uncertainty of **0.1–0.5°**, and possible calibration errors of **2–3°**, can move substantial boundary length among low-angle bins; older work found misorientations ≥20° generally within 5° of truth, with larger relative errors at smaller angles. (muirhead2001themorphologicalcharacterisation pages 37-43, britton2018understandingdeformationwith pages 1-3)

Five-parameter GBCD adds sensitivity to boundary-plane reconstruction, registration, voxel aspect ratio, and angular binning. In a 3D Σ3 analysis, the coherent-twin peak was:

- **240 MRD** at 1:1 spacing without secondary alignment;
- **390 MRD** at 2:1 spacing without that alignment;
- **670 MRD** at 1:1 after secondary alignment;
- **1090 MRD** using both 2:1 spacing and secondary alignment, essentially matching **1100 MRD** from stereology. (rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 4-5)

Changing discretization from 9 to 11 bins per 90° moved the peak to **3600 MRD**, because the ideal twin changed from lying on a bin boundary to lying within a bin. An independent length-based estimate gave **21.9% coherent twins**, while the approximately 1100-MRD reconstruction differed by more than 20% from the corresponding expected peak. GBCD peak intensity is therefore not reproducible without the full discretization and registration specification. (rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 4-5)

## 2. Documented systematic bias

The best-supported directions of bias are:

1. **Minimum-size filtering:** removes fine grains, lowers grain count, and raises number-weighted grain size. It was the dominant source of variation in the titanium round robin. (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 1-9)
2. **Dilation/neighborhood reassignment:** erases small islands, smooths boundaries, and merges them into larger neighbors; grain size rises and boundary length/count usually falls. The exact magnitude depends on map quality and iteration count. (rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 2-4)
3. **Confidence/fit rejection without controlled filling:** creates non-random holes near boundaries and deformed regions; it may fragment grains. Filling those holes may instead bridge genuine boundaries. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 16-20, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26)
4. **Coarser step size:** may miss small grains and narrow boundaries, but in continuously rotating AM grains it can also split grains, producing the observed decrease in reconstructed size. The sign is therefore microstructure-dependent, although the Hastelloy-X series showed decreasing size with coarsening. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16)
5. **Higher reconstruction angle:** systematically merges low-angle domains and raises grain size by roughly 4–6% in the reported Ti test. (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26)
6. **Number weighting:** strongly overweights cleanup-generated or genuine small grains. Area-weighted measures reduced cross-cleanup variation from as much as ±100% to ≤10% in the reported comparison. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10)
7. **Edge-grain exclusion:** without stereological correction, preferentially removes large grains and underestimates area-weighted size in small maps. ISO 13067 recommends Miles–Lantejoul-type correction, although it is difficult for irregular AM grains. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10)
8. **Tilt/drift:** a 2° tilt error produced a predicted area-size factor of **0.95**. Under typical distortion most methods remained within **±0.5 ASTM G**, but strong drift produced changes up to **±2 G** for intercept methods and about **1 G** for planimetric methods; TPC/ASTM E2627-type approaches were most robust. (timberlake2026effectsofsem pages 14-17, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26)
9. **2D sectioning of anisotropic grains:** inflates apparent ODF strength even when the true ODF is uniform. (currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 1-3, currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 9-12)
10. **Angular smoothing and cleanup:** generally lowers KAM/GND and LAGB content by suppressing short-wavelength orientation variations, but can create gradients at interfaces if orientations are inappropriately mixed. No universal correction factor exists.

## 3. Uncertainty quantification and statistical sufficiency

### Grain size

The most complete uncertainty framework treats:

- sampling variability from bootstrap subsampling as **Type A**;
- cleanup range and histogram/bin precision as **Type B**, often rectangular distributions;
- standard components combined in quadrature;
- expanded uncertainty reported with **k=2**.

Using this approach, a relative combined expanded uncertainty near **20%** was considered achievable for AM grain-size measurement. Sampling was usually the dominant component. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16)

For generic grain-size stabilization, synthetic distortion work found curves flattening around **300–500 grains**. ASTM E112's traditional minimum is only **50 grains** for planimetric measurement or 50 intercepts, which is a minimum count rather than assurance of narrow uncertainty. (timberlake2026effectsofsem pages 14-17)

Reported size should include the distribution and uncertainty, not merely a mean. For skewed populations, lognormal/Weibull descriptions, medians, quantiles, and indexed-area-weighted cumulative distributions are preferable to assuming a Gaussian grain-number distribution. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 1-5, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 10-16)

### Texture

The available simulation study used **1000 repeated realizations** to estimate median and 95% critical J-index values. Approximately **2000 independent crystal orientations** were required before sample-count effects became small for the tested uniform ODFs. This is a more relevant sample-size concept than number of EBSD pixels because neighboring pixels within one grain are not independent orientation samples. (currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 9-12)

Confidence intervals for texture should therefore be generated by resampling grains or spatial blocks—not individual pixels—and should include ODF bandwidth uncertainty and, where grain shapes are anisotropic, sectioning/cut bias. Current tools often omit covariance among grain shape, size, and orientation, prompting calls for joint, open, validated stereological inversion. (currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 1-3)

### Misorientation, KAM, GND, and boundary statistics

For these outputs, a practical uncertainty budget should propagate angular precision through the spatial derivative and repeat the analysis over plausible cleanup, neighbor-kernel, and threshold choices. At minimum, report a noise floor such as the Hough/HR GND floors above. Because GND inversion is underdetermined and 2D EBSD measures only part of the curvature tensor, the resulting density is normally a model-dependent lower bound, not a complete dislocation-density measurement. (britton2018understandingdeformationwith pages 1-3, britton2018understandingdeformationwith pages 3-6)

Formal confidence intervals and minimum-grain requirements for KAM, GND, and LAGB/HAGB fractions remain an important literature gap. Spatial block bootstrap, repeated-map designs, and sensitivity envelopes are more defensible than pixel-wise standard errors.

## 4. Interlaboratory and inter-software reproducibility

The VAMAS/ISO-oriented titanium exercise included laboratories from **eight countries**, including three equipment manufacturers, five national metrology institutes, one university, and two industrial laboratories. Four of 12 laboratories produced significantly different results. After outlier removal, between-laboratory reproducibility standard deviations were **1.98 μm** for equivalent-circle diameter and **1.15 μm** for linear intercept. Equivalent-circle values averaged approximately **10% higher** than intercept values. (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 1-9, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 9-11)

Equivalent-circle reproducibility was much poorer: reported reproducibility limits were **R=5.79 μm** for equivalent circle and **R=3.36 μm** for linear intercept, a roughly 70% difference. The causes were magnification calibration, tilt correction, scan geometry/drift, insufficient mapped area, step size, cleanup, and especially minimum-grain cutoff. Within-laboratory repeatability was substantially better than between-laboratory reproducibility. (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 1-9, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 23-26)

An earlier multi-material comparison involving up to nine laboratories also found that only four performed consistently well; identified determinants were SEM resolution, EBSD camera, preparation, and operator skill. (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 9-11)

The newer AM comparison applied a common 10° threshold across AZtecCrystal, OIM Analysis, and MTEX. It found that implementation differences in cleanup and grain-area calculation remain consequential, particularly for number-weighted measures. Area-weighted median MFD was substantially more software-robust. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10)

For GBCD, the same dataset changed from **240 to 1090 MRD** solely through spacing/registration choices and to **3600 MRD** through angular discretization. This is effectively a software/protocol reproducibility warning even though it was not a multi-laboratory round robin. (rohrer2010derivinggrainboundary pages 4-5)

No broadly adopted benchmark or round robin was found that simultaneously compares vendors and laboratories for KAM, GND, LAGB/HAGB fractions, neighbor cleanup, and dictionary-versus-Hough indexing. That absence is itself important: grain-size metrology is relatively mature, while deformation and boundary-character metrics remain mostly method-specific.

## 5. Standards, consensus, and minimum reproducible reporting

ASTM E2627 and ISO 13067 primarily standardize EBSD grain-size measurement, not the full range of KAM/GND, texture, or GBCD analyses. From the standards-oriented studies, the minimum reporting package should include:

1. **Specimen and geometry:** preparation route, analyzed plane/direction, accelerating voltage, current, working distance, nominal and calibrated tilt, scan orientation, distortion/drift correction, and magnification calibration.
2. **Map sampling:** physical map dimensions, grid geometry, step size, field count and selection procedure, indexed fraction, number of points, grains, and edge grains.
3. **Pattern/indexing details:** detector/camera, pattern resolution and binning, exposure, Hough/dictionary/refinement/HR method, phase files, CI/fit/peak thresholds, and angular precision or empirical repeatability.
4. **Cleanup audit trail:** every operation in order, iteration count, neighborhood/kernel, CI or fit criterion, dilation/correlation/fill rule, whether patterns or orientations were averaged, and the fraction of points whose orientation changed. Raw and cleaned maps should both be retained.
5. **Grain reconstruction:** misorientation threshold, point-to-point versus grain-mean rule, treatment of pseudosymmetry/twins, connectivity, minimum-grain cutoff in points and physical units, removed grain count and area fraction, and edge-grain handling.
6. **Statistic:** number-, area-, or point-weighting; equivalent-circle, intercept, Feret, or area metric; complete distribution/quantiles; histogram bins or KDE bandwidth; and uncertainty coverage factor.
7. **KAM/GND:** physical kernel size and neighbor shell, angular cutoff, boundary exclusion, gradient operator, Burgers vector, slip/dislocation basis, inversion norm, smoothing, and detection/noise floor.
8. **Boundary statistics/GBCD:** angular noise cutoff; LAGB/HAGB threshold; length-, segment-, or count-weighting; CSL tolerance; line simplification; bin/discretization; voxel aspect ratio; serial-section registration; and uncertainty/sensitivity analysis.
9. **Texture:** number of independent grains, grain/point/area weighting, specimen and crystal symmetry, ODF kernel/bandwidth, section orientation, texture-strength definition, and confidence interval method.

The strongest consensus is that post-processing must be treated as part of the measurement model. Step size and reconstruction threshold must be reported together; cutoff and cleanup effects should be quantified; cleanup-induced changes should remain within the applicable standard's limits; field-of-view sampling should be included in uncertainty; and raw data plus scripts or complete software recipes should accompany results wherever possible. (tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 5-10, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 16-20, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24, mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 9-11)

The literature explicitly motivates more objective workflows. The titanium round robin demonstrated that operator-selected cutoffs and cleanup dominate between-lab variation. The AM study advocates standardized, software-robust, indexed-area-weighted statistics with bootstrap uncertainty. The texture study calls for open, documented, validated tools that jointly correct grain shape, size, and orientation and provide uncertainty rather than applying separate hidden-assumption corrections. (mingard2012determinationofgrain pages 30-32, tong2026towardsstandardisationof pages 20-24, currier2024towardsanintegrated pages 1-3)

## Bottom line

- **Grain size/count:** highly sensitive unless step size, threshold, cutoff, cleanup, field size, edge treatment, and weighting are fixed. Number-weighted values may change by order-unity amounts; robust area-weighted medians can often be held within about 10% processing sensitivity.
- **Texture/ODF:** orientation precision matters, but independent-grain count, bandwidth, weighting, and 2D sectioning bias can be equally important. Around 2000 independent orientations were needed for stable J-index in the cited synthetic tests.
- **KAM/GND:** among the least transferable EBSD metrics. Conventional versus HR angular precision changes the GND floor by about two orders of magnitude, and step size changes it inversely.
- **LAGB/HAGB:** intrinsically threshold- and precision-dependent; cleanup and angular smoothing preferentially suppress LAGBs.
- **GBCD:** can change by factors of several solely from registration, voxel aspect ratio, and binning; sharp special-boundary peaks require full protocol reporting.
- **Reproducibility:** achievable but not automatic. The Ti round robin had 4/12 significant laboratory outliers; controlled grain-size workflows can approach roughly 20% expanded uncertainty, whereas comparable validated uncertainty frameworks are still lacking for KAM/GND and boundary-character metrics.

# Sensitivity, uncertainty, and reproducibility of EBSD-derived microstructural measurements

## Executive conclusion

EBSD-derived quantities are **not intrinsic outputs of the orientation map alone**. Grain size/count, low-angle versus high-angle boundary fractions, KAM/GND, texture strength, and GBCD are conditional on spatial sampling, orientation precision, indexing, reconstruction, cleanup, censoring, and statistical weighting. The strongest quantitative evidence concerns grain size: plausible operator and software choices can change number-weighted results by **±26–100%**, while carefully constructed area-weighted measures typically vary by **±0.2–10%**. A standards-oriented workflow can achieve a combined expanded uncertainty of roughly **20% at k=2**, but uncontrolled workflows can differ far more. Formal uncertainty studies are substantially less mature for KAM/GND, LAGB/HAGB fractions, texture intensity, and GBCD. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003)

The evidence-supported parameter effects are summarized below.

| Parameter / operation | Affected outputs | Quantified literature result | Direction / mechanism of bias | Reporting / best-practice implication |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EBSD step size | Grain size, grain count, reconstructed connectivity | ISO 13067 recommends step size ≈ 10% of average grain diameter; AM study argues 20% can be too coarse for non-convex grains. In a Hastelloy-X example, binning from 3 μm to 6 μm reduced maximum grain size from 1250 μm to 970 μm, and median plus 75th-percentile minimum Feret diameter decreased systematically as step size increased from 1.25 to 15 μm (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000012) | Larger step size can split thin/non-convex grains by loss of pixel connectivity and changes the effective boundary threshold because misorientation is measured only between adjacent points; reported effect in AM microstructures was a systematic decrease in measured grain size with coarser step size (pqac-00000012) | Always report step size together with grain-boundary threshold angle; comparisons are invalid unless both are identical, especially where subgrain structure or intragranular rotations are present (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003) |
| Grain-boundary misorientation threshold for reconstruction | Grain size, grain count, LAGB/HAGB fractions | In the Ti round robin reanalysis table, using 15° instead of 5° increased measured grain size from 30.5 to 31.8 μm at 0.5 μm step with 2 μm cutoff (+4.3%), from 35.9 to 37.5 μm at 3 μm step with 10 μm cutoff (+4.5%), from 34.9 to 36.9 μm at 3 μm +2° tilt (+5.7%), and from 33.6 to 35.4 μm in another 3 μm condition (+5.4%) (pqac-00000011). AM guidance recommends 10° rather than 5° when subgrain structure is present (pqac-00000007) | Raising the threshold merges more low-angle boundaries into grains, increasing grain size and reducing counted grain number; it also directly shifts LAGB/HAGB fractions because the class boundary is user-defined (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012) | Must report the exact threshold angle used for grain reconstruction and any distinction between grain and subgrain boundaries (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000011) |

In one AM example, only 0.6% of indexed points belonged to grains <10 points, but excluding them still had to be accounted for in cumulative histograms (pqac-00000012) | Removing small grains systematically inflates reported grain size and lowers grain count; effect is strongest for number-weighted statistics and for maps with non-random unindexed boundary pixels (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006) | Report the cutoff in both pixels/points and micrometres, plus the indexed area fraction removed by the cutoff (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003) |
| Indexing fraction, CI/fit thresholding, and cleanup extent | Grain size, grain count, reproducibility | Grain-cleanup uncertainty was ±13% for maps with 65% indexing versus ±4% for maps with 95% indexing (pqac-00000001). In AM inter-software comparisons, number-weighted grain-size metrics varied by ±26–100% with different clean-up methods, while area-weighted metrics varied by only ±0.2–10% (pqac-00000000). One round robin noted acceptable indexing around ~80%, despite a nominal 95% target (pqac-00000002) | Unindexed points are not spatially random; they cluster near boundaries and especially distort small grains, causing artificial fragmentation or linking. Cleanup that reassigns low-confidence points can materially change grain topology (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000011) | Report indexed fraction, CI/fit thresholds, whether low-confidence pixels were removed or reassigned, and the difference between no cleanup and maximum cleanup if used for uncertainty estimation (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000011) |
| Cleanup operations such as grain dilation / reassignment | Grain size, grain count, boundary network, potentially boundary fractions | In 3D GBCD work, data were cleaned with two iterations of grain dilation and a minimum grain size of 10 pixels; groups of <10 pixels with disorientations <5° were reassigned to adjacent grains (pqac-00000015). AM grain-size work notes standards constraints that cleanup should change results by ≤5% (ISO 13067) or ≤10% (ASTM E2627) (pqac-00000000) | These operations systematically erase small grains and smooth/regularize boundaries, tending to increase grain size and reduce grain count unless tightly constrained; they also alter the boundary network used for downstream boundary statistics (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000000) | Cleanup routines should be constrained by standards limits and described explicitly, including iterations and reassignment rules (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015) |

*Table: This table summarizes quantitative literature evidence on how key EBSD acquisition and post-processing choices change grain size, texture, boundary statistics, and orientation-gradient metrics. It is useful as a compact checklist of known sensitivities, systematic biases, and reporting requirements needed for reproducible EBSD analysis.*

## 1. Quantified sensitivity studies

### 1.1 Step size and mapped area

Step size affects both spatial resolution and the *effective* grain-reconstruction criterion. In microstructures with smooth intragranular rotation, the same total rotation is divided among more neighboring points at fine step size; coarsening can therefore make point-to-point misorientation exceed the reconstruction threshold and split a formerly connected grain. Coarse sampling can also disconnect narrow regions of non-convex grains. In an AM Hastelloy-X example, increasing step size from **3 to 6 μm** reduced the maximum reconstructed minimum-Feret diameter from **1250 to 970 μm**. Binning from **1.25 to 15 μm** produced a systematic decline in median and 75th-percentile minimum-Feret diameter. (pqac-00000012)

ISO 13067-oriented guidance is approximately **one step per 10% of mean grain diameter**. A commonly used 20%-of-diameter rule can be inadequate for non-convex AM grains. Step size and boundary threshold are interdependent and must be held fixed for comparisons. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003)

Field of view is at least as important as pixel density. Bootstrap analysis found approximately **10% sampling uncertainty at a field width of 15 grain lengths**, with the mean stabilizing above roughly seven grain lengths but outlier risk remaining. The proposed robust condition is about **20 grain lengths per field of view**, especially for elongated AM grains. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000012)

### 1.2 Grain-reconstruction misorientation tolerance

Increasing the reconstruction threshold merges boundaries and therefore increases mean grain size and decreases grain count. In the titanium round-robin reanalysis, changing the boundary threshold from **5° to 15°** increased mean size:

- **30.5 to 31.8 μm** at 0.5 μm step and 2 μm cutoff: **+4.3%**;
- **35.9 to 37.5 μm** at 3 μm step and 10 μm cutoff: **+4.5%**;
- **34.9 to 36.9 μm** in a tilted condition: **+5.7%**;
- **33.6 to 35.4 μm** in another 3 μm condition: **+5.4%**. (pqac-00000011)

This parameter also directly determines LAGB/HAGB fractions: raising the grain threshold reclassifies or removes boundaries in the interval between the old and new thresholds. Thus a reported “LAGB fraction” is uninterpretable unless the lower noise cutoff, LAGB/HAGB dividing angle, reconstruction rule, and length/segment weighting are stated. For AM structures containing intragranular rotations, 10° has been recommended over 5° for identifying morphological grains, but that is a purpose-dependent convention rather than a universal physical boundary. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000012)

### 1.3 Minimum-grain cutoff and grain weighting

The minimum accepted grain size was the **largest identified source of interlaboratory variation** in the titanium round robin. Small grains disproportionately affect number-weighted means, and the effect depends on step size, indexing quality, and treatment of unindexed points. ISO 13067 and ASTM E2627 were reported as using markedly different exclusion scales—approximately **10 points** and **100 points**, respectively—so “standard-compliant” analyses can still differ unless the standard and implementation are specified. Cutoffs should be reported in both pixels and physical units. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006)

The direction of bias is systematic: removing small grains lowers grain count and raises number-weighted mean grain size. In inter-software AM analyses, changing cleanup produced **±26–100%** changes in number-weighted metrics but only **±0.2–10%** in area-weighted metrics. Indexed-area-weighted median minimum-Feret diameter is consequently much more robust than a number mean. (pqac-00000000)

In one AM dataset, indexed-area-weighted medians had half-ranges of only **±1.5% for MFD** and **±9.3% for grain area**. Conventional area-weighted medians varied by **±16%** and **±33%**, respectively, because field-size, edge, and cutoff effects were not fully represented. (pqac-00000012)

### 1.4 Indexing fraction, confidence/fit thresholds, and cleanup

Cleanup sensitivity rises sharply as raw map quality declines. Estimated cleanup uncertainty was **±13% at 65% indexing**, compared with **±4% at 95% indexing**. Unindexed points are generally not missing at random; they concentrate at boundaries, deformed areas, fine features, and weak patterns. Depending on topology, they can fragment one grain into several or allow adjacent grains to be linked after filling. (pqac-00000001)

The titanium round robin compared systems that either indexed every point with a confidence measure or left points unindexed when fit criteria failed. One reanalysis rendered points with **confidence index <0.1** unindexed. This illustrates why “indexing percentage” cannot be compared independently of the CI or fit threshold and indexing philosophy. Approximately 80% indexing was workable in that particular round robin despite a nominal 95% target, but it was not evidence that 80% is generally sufficient. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000011)

Grain dilation is explicitly topology-changing. One 3D GBCD workflow used **two iterations**, a **10-pixel minimum grain**, and reassigned groups below 10 pixels whose disorientation was below **5°** to an adjacent grain. Such processing erases small components and modifies boundary geometry; it is not neutral denoising. (pqac-00000015)

The standards-oriented limits reported in the AM study were that cleanup should alter results by no more than **5% under ISO 13067** or **10% under ASTM E2627**. These limits should be treated as acceptance checks, not proof that the cleaned map is unbiased. (pqac-00000000)

Direct controlled, transferable numerical studies for **neighbor orientation correlation, neighbor pattern averaging, and vendor-specific CI standardization** were not found in the retrieved quantitative literature. Their expected directions are nevertheless clear: orientation-correlation filling and dilation remove isolated grains and shorten or move boundaries; neighbor-pattern averaging improves signal-to-noise but mixes patterns across boundaries unless boundary-aware, degrading spatial resolution and potentially suppressing narrow grains and LAGBs. Because the magnitude is dataset- and implementation-specific, it should be measured by raw-versus-processed parameter sweeps rather than assumed.

### 1.5 Indexing method and orientation precision: Hough, refinement, and HR-EBSD

Conventional Hough EBSD has reported absolute-orientation accuracy of roughly **2°** and relative misorientation precision of approximately **0.1–0.5°**. Cross-correlation HR-EBSD reaches about **0.006°**, an improvement of roughly two orders of magnitude. This difference changes the noise floor of every local-misorientation-derived quantity. (pqac-00000013)

For Burgers vector magnitude 0.3 nm, estimated measurable GND floors at **1 μm step** are above approximately **3×10¹³ m⁻²** for conventional Hough EBSD and **3×10¹¹ m⁻²** for HR-EBSD. At **100 nm step**, the corresponding floors rise to **3×10¹⁴** and **3×10¹² m⁻²** because curvature divides angular error by spatial separation. (pqac-00000013)

HR-EBSD also has analysis choices: reference and test patterns should remain within roughly **12°** for adequate overlap; normalized cross-correlation peak height below **0.3** indicates an unreliable result in simulations; and omitting rotational remapping can generate artificially high stresses. GND inversion is underdetermined and produces a lower-bound solution conditional on the selected dislocation types and optimization norm. (pqac-00000014)

The retrieved full-text evidence did not support a defensible universal numerical conversion between **Hough, dictionary indexing, and full-pattern orientation refinement** for grain size, texture intensity, or GBCD. The robust conclusion is narrower: full-pattern/cross-correlation refinement greatly reduces relative angular noise and therefore materially changes KAM/GND and near-threshold LAGB statistics, whereas grain topology will change mainly where Hough misindexing or angular error lies near the chosen reconstruction threshold. Method, pattern resolution/binning, refinement model, and quality rejection threshold must therefore be reported.

### 1.6 KAM and GND density

KAM is particularly parameter-dependent because it is an average over a user-defined neighborhood, normally after rejecting neighbor pairs above a chosen angle. Changing step size changes the physical kernel radius; changing neighbor order changes spatial smoothing; changing the exclusion angle changes whether boundaries and subboundaries enter the calculation; cleanup suppresses isolated angular outliers and therefore usually lowers KAM. GND density additionally scales as orientation gradient, approximately angular change divided by step length, so its noise floor rises as step size decreases unless angular precision improves proportionally. The Hough-versus-HR floors above quantify this effect. (pqac-00000013)

Consequently, KAM or GND values are not reproducible if only “KAM was calculated” is reported. Required information includes step size, neighbor shell/kernel and physical radius, boundary exclusion angle, whether zero/unindexed neighbors are omitted, indexing/refinement method and angular precision, smoothing or cleanup, Burgers vector, finite-difference scheme, assumed slip/dislocation systems, inversion norm, and whether the value is a lower bound. The retrieved corpus contained no mature interlaboratory uncertainty standard for KAM/GND comparable to ASTM E2627 or ISO 13067 for grain size.

### 1.7 Texture strength and ODF intensity

Texture has two separable sensitivities: orientation-measurement error and statistical/sectioning bias. Synthetic sectioning showed that even a truly uniform 3D ODF can acquire a nonuniform 2D EBSD ODF because elongated grains are more likely to be intersected when their long axes are near the section normal. This systematically inflates apparent fabric strength; it is not random angular noise. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009)

For repeated synthetic trials, the J-index decreased toward its asymptote as grain count increased; above approximately **2000 crystal orientations**, further sample-size effect was minimal. ODFs based on **3000 grains** could nevertheless retain morphology-driven cut bias. Kernel optimization also generated small “stair-step” changes in J-index as sample size changed, demonstrating that ODF bandwidth is itself a processing parameter. (pqac-00000009)

Thus texture reporting should specify whether orientations are point-, grain-, or area-weighted; number of independent grains and points; ODF kernel/bandwidth and symmetry; section orientation; grain-shape anisotropy; and any smoothing or removal of low-quality points. Point weighting overrepresents large grains, while one-orientation-per-grain weighting gives each grain equal weight. Neither is universally correct; the estimand must be declared.

### 1.8 Boundary fractions and GBCD

LAGB/HAGB fractions are highly sensitive near both the angular-resolution floor and the chosen class boundary. Conventional Hough uncertainty of **0.1–0.5°**, and possible calibration errors of **2–3°**, can move substantial boundary length among low-angle bins; older work found misorientations ≥20° generally within 5° of truth, with larger relative errors at smaller angles. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000013)

Five-parameter GBCD adds sensitivity to boundary-plane reconstruction, registration, voxel aspect ratio, and angular binning. In a 3D Σ3 analysis, the coherent-twin peak was:

- **240 MRD** at 1:1 spacing without secondary alignment;
- **390 MRD** at 2:1 spacing without that alignment;
- **670 MRD** at 1:1 after secondary alignment;
- **1090 MRD** using both 2:1 spacing and secondary alignment, essentially matching **1100 MRD** from stereology. (pqac-00000016)

Changing discretization from 9 to 11 bins per 90° moved the peak to **3600 MRD**, because the ideal twin changed from lying on a bin boundary to lying within a bin. An independent length-based estimate gave **21.9% coherent twins**, while the approximately 1100-MRD reconstruction differed by more than 20% from the corresponding expected peak. GBCD peak intensity is therefore not reproducible without the full discretization and registration specification. (pqac-00000016)

## 2. Documented systematic bias

The best-supported directions of bias are:

1. **Minimum-size filtering:** removes fine grains, lowers grain count, and raises number-weighted grain size. It was the dominant source of variation in the titanium round robin. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006)
2. **Dilation/neighborhood reassignment:** erases small islands, smooths boundaries, and merges them into larger neighbors; grain size rises and boundary length/count usually falls. The exact magnitude depends on map quality and iteration count. (pqac-00000015)
3. **Confidence/fit rejection without controlled filling:** creates non-random holes near boundaries and deformed regions; it may fragment grains. Filling those holes may instead bridge genuine boundaries. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000011)
4. **Coarser step size:** may miss small grains and narrow boundaries, but in continuously rotating AM grains it can also split grains, producing the observed decrease in reconstructed size. The sign is therefore microstructure-dependent, although the Hastelloy-X series showed decreasing size with coarsening. (pqac-00000012)
5. **Higher reconstruction angle:** systematically merges low-angle domains and raises grain size by roughly 4–6% in the reported Ti test. (pqac-00000011)
6. **Number weighting:** strongly overweights cleanup-generated or genuine small grains. Area-weighted measures reduced cross-cleanup variation from as much as ±100% to ≤10% in the reported comparison. (pqac-00000000)
7. **Edge-grain exclusion:** without stereological correction, preferentially removes large grains and underestimates area-weighted size in small maps. ISO 13067 recommends Miles–Lantejoul-type correction, although it is difficult for irregular AM grains. (pqac-00000000)
8. **Tilt/drift:** a 2° tilt error produced a predicted area-size factor of **0.95**. Under typical distortion most methods remained within **±0.5 ASTM G**, but strong drift produced changes up to **±2 G** for intercept methods and about **1 G** for planimetric methods; TPC/ASTM E2627-type approaches were most robust. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000011)
9. **2D sectioning of anisotropic grains:** inflates apparent ODF strength even when the true ODF is uniform. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009)
10. **Angular smoothing and cleanup:** generally lowers KAM/GND and LAGB content by suppressing short-wavelength orientation variations, but can create gradients at interfaces if orientations are inappropriately mixed. No universal correction factor exists.

## 3. Uncertainty quantification and statistical sufficiency

### Grain size

The most complete uncertainty framework treats:

- sampling variability from bootstrap subsampling as **Type A**;
- cleanup range and histogram/bin precision as **Type B**, often rectangular distributions;
- standard components combined in quadrature;
- expanded uncertainty reported with **k=2**.

Using this approach, a relative combined expanded uncertainty near **20%** was considered achievable for AM grain-size measurement. Sampling was usually the dominant component. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000012)

For generic grain-size stabilization, synthetic distortion work found curves flattening around **300–500 grains**. ASTM E112's traditional minimum is only **50 grains** for planimetric measurement or 50 intercepts, which is a minimum count rather than assurance of narrow uncertainty. (pqac-00000004)

Reported size should include the distribution and uncertainty, not merely a mean. For skewed populations, lognormal/Weibull descriptions, medians, quantiles, and indexed-area-weighted cumulative distributions are preferable to assuming a Gaussian grain-number distribution. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000012)

### Texture

The available simulation study used **1000 repeated realizations** to estimate median and 95% critical J-index values. Approximately **2000 independent crystal orientations** were required before sample-count effects became small for the tested uniform ODFs. This is a more relevant sample-size concept than number of EBSD pixels because neighboring pixels within one grain are not independent orientation samples. (pqac-00000009)

Confidence intervals for texture should therefore be generated by resampling grains or spatial blocks—not individual pixels—and should include ODF bandwidth uncertainty and, where grain shapes are anisotropic, sectioning/cut bias. Current tools often omit covariance among grain shape, size, and orientation, prompting calls for joint, open, validated stereological inversion. (pqac-00000008)

### Misorientation, KAM, GND, and boundary statistics

For these outputs, a practical uncertainty budget should propagate angular precision through the spatial derivative and repeat the analysis over plausible cleanup, neighbor-kernel, and threshold choices. At minimum, report a noise floor such as the Hough/HR GND floors above. Because GND inversion is underdetermined and 2D EBSD measures only part of the curvature tensor, the resulting density is normally a model-dependent lower bound, not a complete dislocation-density measurement. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014)

Formal confidence intervals and minimum-grain requirements for KAM, GND, and LAGB/HAGB fractions remain an important literature gap. Spatial block bootstrap, repeated-map designs, and sensitivity envelopes are more defensible than pixel-wise standard errors.

## 4. Interlaboratory and inter-software reproducibility

The VAMAS/ISO-oriented titanium exercise included laboratories from **eight countries**, including three equipment manufacturers, five national metrology institutes, one university, and two industrial laboratories. Four of 12 laboratories produced significantly different results. After outlier removal, between-laboratory reproducibility standard deviations were **1.98 μm** for equivalent-circle diameter and **1.15 μm** for linear intercept. Equivalent-circle values averaged approximately **10% higher** than intercept values. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000010)

Equivalent-circle reproducibility was much poorer: reported reproducibility limits were **R=5.79 μm** for equivalent circle and **R=3.36 μm** for linear intercept, a roughly 70% difference. The causes were magnification calibration, tilt correction, scan geometry/drift, insufficient mapped area, step size, cleanup, and especially minimum-grain cutoff. Within-laboratory repeatability was substantially better than between-laboratory reproducibility. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011)

An earlier multi-material comparison involving up to nine laboratories also found that only four performed consistently well; identified determinants were SEM resolution, EBSD camera, preparation, and operator skill. (pqac-00000010)

The newer AM comparison applied a common 10° threshold across AZtecCrystal, OIM Analysis, and MTEX. It found that implementation differences in cleanup and grain-area calculation remain consequential, particularly for number-weighted measures. Area-weighted median MFD was substantially more software-robust. (pqac-00000000)

For GBCD, the same dataset changed from **240 to 1090 MRD** solely through spacing/registration choices and to **3600 MRD** through angular discretization. This is effectively a software/protocol reproducibility warning even though it was not a multi-laboratory round robin. (pqac-00000016)

No broadly adopted benchmark or round robin was found that simultaneously compares vendors and laboratories for KAM, GND, LAGB/HAGB fractions, neighbor cleanup, and dictionary-versus-Hough indexing. That absence is itself important: grain-size metrology is relatively mature, while deformation and boundary-character metrics remain mostly method-specific.

## 5. Standards, consensus, and minimum reproducible reporting

ASTM E2627 and ISO 13067 primarily standardize EBSD grain-size measurement, not the full range of KAM/GND, texture, or GBCD analyses. From the standards-oriented studies, the minimum reporting package should include:

1. **Specimen and geometry:** preparation route, analyzed plane/direction, accelerating voltage, current, working distance, nominal and calibrated tilt, scan orientation, distortion/drift correction, and magnification calibration.
2. **Map sampling:** physical map dimensions, grid geometry, step size, field count and selection procedure, indexed fraction, number of points, grains, and edge grains.
3. **Pattern/indexing details:** detector/camera, pattern resolution and binning, exposure, Hough/dictionary/refinement/HR method, phase files, CI/fit/peak thresholds, and angular precision or empirical repeatability.
4. **Cleanup audit trail:** every operation in order, iteration count, neighborhood/kernel, CI or fit criterion, dilation/correlation/fill rule, whether patterns or orientations were averaged, and the fraction of points whose orientation changed. Raw and cleaned maps should both be retained.
5. **Grain reconstruction:** misorientation threshold, point-to-point versus grain-mean rule, treatment of pseudosymmetry/twins, connectivity, minimum-grain cutoff in points and physical units, removed grain count and area fraction, and edge-grain handling.
6. **Statistic:** number-, area-, or point-weighting; equivalent-circle, intercept, Feret, or area metric; complete distribution/quantiles; histogram bins or KDE bandwidth; and uncertainty coverage factor.
7. **KAM/GND:** physical kernel size and neighbor shell, angular cutoff, boundary exclusion, gradient operator, Burgers vector, slip/dislocation basis, inversion norm, smoothing, and detection/noise floor.
8. **Boundary statistics/GBCD:** angular noise cutoff; LAGB/HAGB threshold; length-, segment-, or count-weighting; CSL tolerance; line simplification; bin/discretization; voxel aspect ratio; serial-section registration; and uncertainty/sensitivity analysis.
9. **Texture:** number of independent grains, grain/point/area weighting, specimen and crystal symmetry, ODF kernel/bandwidth, section orientation, texture-strength definition, and confidence interval method.

The strongest consensus is that post-processing must be treated as part of the measurement model. Step size and reconstruction threshold must be reported together; cutoff and cleanup effects should be quantified; cleanup-induced changes should remain within the applicable standard's limits; field-of-view sampling should be included in uncertainty; and raw data plus scripts or complete software recipes should accompany results wherever possible. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000010)

The literature explicitly motivates more objective workflows. The titanium round robin demonstrated that operator-selected cutoffs and cleanup dominate between-lab variation. The AM study advocates standardized, software-robust, indexed-area-weighted statistics with bootstrap uncertainty. The texture study calls for open, documented, validated tools that jointly correct grain shape, size, and orientation and provide uncertainty rather than applying separate hidden-assumption corrections. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000008)

## Bottom line

- **Grain size/count:** highly sensitive unless step size, threshold, cutoff, cleanup, field size, edge treatment, and weighting are fixed. Number-weighted values may change by order-unity amounts; robust area-weighted medians can often be held within about 10% processing sensitivity.
- **Texture/ODF:** orientation precision matters, but independent-grain count, bandwidth, weighting, and 2D sectioning bias can be equally important. Around 2000 independent orientations were needed for stable J-index in the cited synthetic tests.
- **KAM/GND:** among the least transferable EBSD metrics. Conventional versus HR angular precision changes the GND floor by about two orders of magnitude, and step size changes it inversely.
- **LAGB/HAGB:** intrinsically threshold- and precision-dependent; cleanup and angular smoothing preferentially suppress LAGBs.
- **GBCD:** can change by factors of several solely from registration, voxel aspect ratio, and binning; sharp special-boundary peaks require full protocol reporting.
- **Reproducibility:** achievable but not automatic. The Ti round robin had 4/12 significant laboratory outliers; controlled grain-size workflows can approach roughly 20% expanded uncertainty, whereas comparable validated uncertainty frameworks are still lacking for KAM/GND and boundary-character metrics.

contexts.context: The excerpt addresses sensitivity and uncertainty of EBSD-derived grain size measurements across different software packages (AZtecCrystal, OIM Analysis, MTEX 6.0.0) using identical grain boundary threshold angles of 10°. Key findings include: number-weighted metrics show ±26-100% variation with different clean-up methods, while area-weighted metrics are more robust at ±0.2-10% variation. Clean-up routines must comply with ISO 13067 (≤5% change) or ASTM E2627 (≤10% change). Grain area computation method uncertainty is comparable to clean-up effects but has negligible impact on mean free distance (MFD). Standards specify minimum grain size thresholds of 10 points (ISO 13067) or 100 points (ASTM E2627) for exclusion. Edge grain exclusion causes underestimation of area-weighted grain size in small maps, particularly when grain sizes are large relative to map field of view. The Miles-Lantejoul correction is recommended by ISO 13067 to account for edge bias but is complex to implement in additively manufactured microstructures with variable grain shapes.

contexts.context: This interlaboratory round-robin study on titanium grain size measurement via EBSD identified critical sensitivity to multiple parameters. Four of twelve laboratories reported significantly different results. Key error sources included: magnification calibration errors, noise reduction/data cleanup procedures, and step size selection with insufficient mapped area causing larger grains to be missed. After outlier removal, reproducibility standard deviation was 1.98 µm for equivalent circle diameter and 1.15 µm for linear intercept, with 10% lower values for linear intercept measurements. Smallest grain size cutoff choice was identified as the main source of interlaboratory variation, with disproportionate effects from small grains. Calibration and tilt angle measurement errors perpendicular to the tilt axis contributed to area-based measurements. Acceptable indexing was achieved at approximately 80% rather than the stated 95% target. The study emphasized proper reporting of grain size distribution data and cutoff values in both pixels and micrometers.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides quantitative guidance on EBSD grain size measurement uncertainty and reproducibility for additively manufactured materials. Key parameter sensitivities include: EBSD step size should be ~10% of average grain diameter (per ISO 13067), though 20% is too coarse for AM structures with non-convex grains. Field of view (FoV) significantly affects sampling uncertainty—20 grain lengths per FoV achieves ~10% sampling uncertainty, which dominates total combined uncertainty. Random sampling uncertainty is the primary uncertainty component. The indexed-area-weighted median minimum Feret diameter (MFD) is recommended as the primary grain size statistic. EBSD map clean-up operations can change orientations by up to 5%. A relative combined expanded uncertainty (k=2) of 20% is achievable. Grain boundary threshold angle and EBSD step size must be reported when sub-grain structure or intragranular misorientations are present. Edge grains should be excluded. Small grain exclusion requires documenting their indexed area fraction. FoV should be at least 20× larger than median grain length to avoid discrete jumps in cumulative histograms at the 50% median point.

contexts.context: The excerpt addresses sensitivity and reproducibility of EBSD grain size measurements in additively manufactured materials. Key findings include: EBSD average grain size measurements are extremely sensitive to operator choices in experimental design, data clean-up, grain reconstruction, and statistical analysis. Critical parameters and their effects are documented: (1) Small grain removal (< 10-100 points per grain) severely biases results; (2) Step size should be 20 points per grain (20% of average diameter), not 80-500 points; (3) Map quality must exceed 90% indexed fraction, as unindexed points along boundaries artificially fragment or link grains; (4) Misorientation threshold of 10° is more appropriate than 5° for sub-grain structures; (5) Field of view should match grain aspect ratio; (6) Statistics should use log-normal or Weibull distributions rather than Gaussian; (7) Area-weighted means are preferable to number-weighted means which underestimate grain size. An interlaboratory comparison study was conducted to evaluate current practices across software packages (OIM Analysis, AZtecCrystal, MTEX).

contexts.context: The excerpt provides quantitative comparisons between conventional EBSD and HR-EBSD techniques. Conventional Hough-based EBSD achieves absolute orientation accuracy of ~2° and misorientation precision of ~0.1 to 0.5°, while HR-EBSD achieves ~0.006° (1×10⁻⁴ rads) misorientation precision—a two-orders-of-magnitude improvement. ## Summary

This preprint addresses stereological challenges in EBSD-derived textural analysis. The authors note that while EBSD provides "3D orientation of 2D grain sections," **no stereological corrections are typically applied** to EBSD data, unlike traditional thin-section methods. They identify a "fabric cut effect" where crystals oriented perpendicular to the thin section are preferentially sampled, biasing orientation data. The authors argue that existing stereological correction tools (CSDCorrections, CSDslice, ShapeCalc) rely on "simplifying, but hidden, assumptions" and "do not provide the full uncertainty covariance matrix between shape, size, and orientation." They call for an "open source, well-documented, validated, and extendable textural analysis toolkit" enabling simultaneous correction of crystal shape, size, and orientation with "accurate uncertainty estimates." The excerpt does not provide quantified sensitivity studies, documented bias magnitudes, uncertainty quantification methodology, interlaboratory reproducibility data, or community standards compliance details.

# Summary

This excerpt does not address EBSD (Electron Backscatter Diffraction) microstructural measurements or their sensitivity to acquisition and post-processing parameters. Instead, it focuses on the "fabric-cut effect"—how crystal sectioning artifacts affect measured crystallographic texture in optical/manual analyses of geological samples.

The work quantifies texture strength using the J-Index (ranging from 1 for uniform to infinity for single crystal) across synthetic datasets. Key findings include:

- **Sample size effects**: J-Index decreases asymptotically with increasing crystal count; beyond ~2000 orientations, fabric-cut effects plateau (Figure 5)
- **Crystal symmetry**: Negligible first-order effect when comparing orthorhombic vs. triclinic systems at n=3000 (Figure 6)
- **Crystal shape**: More prismatic morphologies produce stronger fabric-cut artifacts (Figure 7)

This excerpt does not contain quantitative sensitivity analyses, uncertainty quantification, bias documentation, or interlaboratory reproducibility studies relevant to EBSD parameter choices or standards (ASTM E2627, ISO 13067).
